title: Symbolic Physical Laws Discovery
book: T. Lazebnik, Computational Methods for Symbolic Physical Laws Discovery (forthcoming)

book_parts.author: Teddy Lazebnik
book_parts.title: Computational Methods for Symbolic Physical Laws Discovery

description: An open course on discovering physical laws with computers: how symbolic regression searches for equations, how physics knowledge guides it, and how to tell a fitted formula from a law. 10 modules, one per chapter of Teddy Lazebnik's forthcoming book, with long videos, slides and browser labs.

modules.title: From predictive models to scientific laws
modules.sub: Why science wants equations, not only good predictions
modules.summary: Why does science want equations, and not only good predictions? A curve that fits can still be wrong about the world. We trace how mathematics became the language of physics, from Archimedes to quantum mechanics, and how computers joined the search for equations. Then we look inside symbolic regression: the space of formulas it searches, how fast that space grows, the seven decisions between observations and an equation, and what makes an equation useful. A worked example with our own falling-ball data puts it to work, eight failure modes show how discoveries can be fake, and a ladder of five claims says how far an equation has climbed.
modules.goal: tell a fitted curve from a candidate law, describe what symbolic regression searches and why its language must be reported, and design the measurement that separates two competing laws.

modules.title: Mathematical languages for symbolic models
modules.summary: Before any search begins, someone chooses a language. We follow mathematical notation from words to symbols to computation, then store one formula as a tree, as prefix and postfix strings, as a graph with sharing, as a token sequence and as a grammar derivation, and see what each makes easy, hard or invalid. Grammars and unit rules decide what may be written; our exact count shows how much of the space units remove. The second video turns to constants (fitting, redundancy, and whether 6.296 is really 2π), to the many disguises of one formula, and to complexity measures that disagree. It ends by designing a language for a pendulum with air drag, before touching any data.
modules.goal: store and measure formulas in several representations, write a grammar with unit rules, fit and question constants, define equivalence for your problem, and declare a complexity measure in advance.

modules.title: Encoding physics and domain knowledge
modules.sub: Units, conservation, symmetry and known pieces
modules.summary: Before any data arrive, we usually know a lot: units, what is conserved, which symmetries hold, the shape of a response, values at a boundary, limiting behaviour, part of the mechanism. This module turns that knowledge into code. With a draining tank as the running example, we sort eight kinds of knowledge, inject the same rule four ways (hard, soft, preferential, after the search), and use units to type-check every node and to shrink five variables to three dimensionless groups. The second video adds conservation (integrating beats differentiating; an unknown invariant found from trajectories), symmetry through invariant variables, shape constraints with a range, boundaries, limits and skeletons, diagnostics for wrong knowledge, and a ladder of knowledge whose every rung is measured.
modules.goal: classify prior knowledge, choose how strongly to encode it, find dimensionless groups, and measure what each piece of knowledge buys with weight paths and ablations.

modules.title: Search and optimization
modules.sub: How the search moves through equation space
modules.summary: Equation space is huge and rough: one edit can change everything, and many change nothing. With the range of a thrown ball as the running example, we count the space exactly (729,657 trees up to eight nodes, 107,570 different candidates), enumerate it with pruning, and evolve formulas with genetic programming: selection, crossover, mutation, diversity and bloat. A race on one budget, repeated over 100 runs on five sets of throws, shows how much a single data set or ten seeds can mislead. Then the other families: token-by-token policies and tree search, pretrained and differentiable generators, constants fitted inside the loop, Pareto fronts, caching and quick checks, stopping rules, and how to compare searchers fairly.
modules.goal: explain how enumeration, genetic programming and sequential or learned searchers move through equation space, fit constants inside the loop, keep a Pareto front, and design a fair comparison with enough seeds, data sets and ablations.

modules.title: Scientific data, noise and experimental design
modules.summary: The data decide which laws can be told apart. With a weight on a spring filmed by a phone, we ask whether data are adequate for a claim (quantity, coverage, resolution, signal to noise, observability, excitation), sort the kinds of noise and sampling trouble from aliasing to gaps with geometry, and follow positions into velocities and accelerations: finite differences turn a millimetre of tracking noise into acceleration noise more than twice the real signal, smoothing trades noise for bias, and weak forms move the derivative onto a known test function. The second video separates new evidence from synthetic data, chooses the next experiment where candidate laws disagree, matches validation splits to the claim, and locks the data decisions in a readiness protocol before the search.
modules.goal: judge whether data are adequate for a discovery claim, diagnose noise and sampling problems, choose between finite differences, smoothing and weak forms, control synthetic data, design the next experiment, and match the validation split to the claim.

modules.title: Static laws and interpretable surrogates
modules.summary: Many laws are static: one formula from inputs to an output. With pendulums timed on Earth, Mars and the Moon and a cyclist's power against speed, we separate candidate laws, empirical correlations and surrogates, and let units work before any search: five quantities become two numbers, and nine pendulums collapse onto one curve. We search a correlation instead of guessing a template, size it from a Pareto front, and test closures inside the simulation they live in, where two equally good fits stop a coasting bike 15 seconds apart. Then we learn what a theory misses with residual laws, build symbolic surrogates and multi-fidelity models, and declare and attack each formula's validity envelope, side by side with black boxes.
modules.goal: tell a law from a correlation and a surrogate, use dimensional analysis and data collapse, search and size a correlation, test a closure inside its simulation, learn a residual law, and state and stress-test a validity envelope.

modules.title: Ordinary differential equations
modules.sub: Discovering how systems change in time
modules.summary: Most laws in physics, chemistry and biology say how a system changes in time. With a simulated chemical clock (the Brusselator, a textbook model of oscillating reactions) we treat every derivative as an estimate and compare finite differences, smoothing and the weak form; find a sparse right-hand side from a library of candidate terms, with a threshold that works across a wide window; compare derivative, weak-form and trajectory matching; and design data that cover the state space, with the feed rate written into the law. Then we test the law where the fit never looked: we rebuild a hidden species from partial knowledge, check steady states and the onset of ticking (a Hopf bifurcation), push the feed beyond the data, and handle noise inside the reaction, a slow detector and a pump that varies the feed.
modules.goal: treat derivatives as estimates, find a sparse right-hand side, choose a formulation, design data that cover the state space and put parameters in the library, rebuild hidden variables from partial knowledge, and validate a dynamical law on steady states, stability and bifurcations, with noise, delays and inputs in the model.

modules.title: PDEs, fields and graphs
modules.summary: Many laws live in space as well as time: a temperature in a solid, a concentration in a fluid, a plant spreading along a coast. With our own simulations of a plant on a 100-km coast (the Fisher–KPP equation) we see why second derivatives from noisy sensors fail, and how the weak form in space and time avoids them; read initial and boundary conditions as evidence, since one front sliding through a window looks like drift; check conservation without derivatives; and choose among plausible laws with an experiment the fit never saw. Then the plant moves to forty ponds with no grid at all: spread becomes a sum over neighbours on a graph, the edges become part of the model, a delay offered to the search turns out to come from the noise, the law transfers to a new map, and a beetle that eats the plant shows what coupled fields need from the data.
modules.goal: estimate what a field law needs and use the weak form in space and time, read initial and boundary conditions as evidence, check conservation, choose among plausible laws with held-out experiments, write laws on graphs with the edges as part of the model, test delays with a negative control, transfer a graph law to a new map, and report benchmarks you can trust.

modules.title: Trustworthy equation discovery
modules.summary: A found law is a claim, and a claim needs its uncertainty, its tests and its record. With our own simulations of a tank draining through a small hole (Torricelli's law) we separate four sources of uncertainty; check whether error bars are calibrated by repeating the experiment in simulation; meet parameters the data can never separate and a short experiment where 79 different formulas fit; and count one law written 61 ways as one. Then we test like we mean it: 21 pipelines, splits that match the claim, a polynomial that summarises but can't predict, a bigger hole and a syrup, strong baselines, negative and positive controls and ablations. Finally we design the experiment that falsifies rival laws, close the loop, put physical sense and stability on the Pareto front, record what reproducibility needs, and keep people in the loop.
modules.goal: name and check the four sources of uncertainty, test calibration, recognise structural and practical non-identifiability and equivalent formulas, run many pipelines and splits that match the claim, use shift tests, baselines, controls and ablations, design discriminating experiments, and report results that others can reproduce.

modules.title: Extensions of symbolic regression
modules.summary: Symbolic regression rarely works alone. We describe a tool by its interface: data with units and claims in; candidates, uncertainty, tests and a log out. On eight textbook laws measured in a narrow range, a one-shot search that keeps the best fit got 131 of 160 right; a small loop that proposes the simplest formula and lets three critics (units, fit to the noise, a wider range) check it got all 160, with about two tool calls per task, and ablations show what each critic does. Then we distil black boxes: a neural network and boosted trees learn a projectile's range, and symbolic students fitted to their answers recover the law where the teachers learned, and copy their mistakes where they did not. One found feature lets a straight line beat both black boxes, a representation bank picks it out, and data from a generative model corrupt the search. We end with research directions and the questions of the whole course.
modules.goal: describe a discovery tool by its interface, build a loop with critics and evaluate it on known answers with costs, abstentions and ablations, distil a black box into a formula and report fidelity and accuracy separately, use found formulas as features, and keep generated data out of the evidence.

episodes.title: A curve is not a law
episodes.hook: Two formulas fit a cooling cup equally well. One of them is a law.
episodes.takeaway: A quartic and an exponential fit five minutes of our cooling cup; after an hour the exponential says 20.2 °C and the quartic almost half a million. Prediction is evidence, not the end point.

transcript.title: Two formulas, one data set
transcript.text: Here are some measurements: the temperature of a cup of coffee, every fifteen seconds, for five minutes. And here are two formulas that fit them. One is a flexible polynomial. The other is a simple exponential. On these points, the polynomial actually fits slightly better. Now ask both formulas the same question. How hot will the cup be in half an hour? The exponential says 23.5 degrees. The polynomial says almost 24,000 degrees. Same data, same quality of fit, very different claims about the world. This whole course lives in the gap between those two formulas. A curve that fits is not yet a law.

transcript.title: Welcome to the course
transcript.text: Welcome to Symbolic Physical Laws Discovery. I'm Teddy. In this course we'll learn how computers can help us find equations, and how to tell when an equation deserves to be called a law. The course follows my upcoming book, chapter by chapter. There are ten modules and twenty two long videos. Every module also has a slide deck, and a lab you can run in your browser. You don't need the book to follow along. Some calculus, a little statistics, and curiosity are enough. This first video is about the target. Before we search for equations, we should agree on what we're looking for. We'll start with history: how mathematics became the language of physics. Then we'll see where computers joined the story. Then we'll separate prediction from explanation. And we'll finish with a question. What does it take for a formula to earn the word law?

transcript.title: How mathematics became the language of physics
transcript.text: People measured the world long before physics existed. They counted, surveyed land, tracked the seasons, and predicted eclipses. The Greeks added something new: proof. A claim in geometry was not just calculated. It was demonstrated, step by step, from definitions. But for a long time, mathematics described nature without explaining it. Explaining was the job of natural philosophy: causes, purposes, why things change. Archimedes crossed that line. His law of the lever turns a plank, a pivot and two weights into a relation you can prove. Weight times distance on one side equals weight times distance on the other. Astronomy took a different path. Ptolemy built a system of circles riding on circles, and it predicted the positions of the planets remarkably well. This was called saving the phenomena: reproducing what you observe. Whether those circles actually existed up there was a separate question. Keep that distinction in mind, because it's the heart of this course. A model that calculates correctly is not the same as a theory of what is real. The work continued across the Islamic world. Ibn al-Haytham, for example, brought geometry and careful experiments together in the study of light and vision. In the sixteenth century, Copernicus put the Sun at the center, partly because it gave the planets a more coherent mathematical order. Then Kepler took Tycho Brahe's careful observations of Mars seriously. The best circular scheme missed them by about eight minutes of arc. That's about a quarter of the Moon's width in the sky. Kepler refused to ignore that tiny gap. He let the data break the circle, and he found the ellipse. Here is the lesson for us. A compact regularity is powerful because it changes which mechanisms are even plausible. Ellipses demanded a physical cause. In 1623, Galileo wrote that the book of nature is written in the language of mathematics. Mathematics had described nature for centuries. What changed was its job. It was becoming the method for finding the structure of physical processes, like falling bodies and flying cannonballs. In 1687, Newton's Principia completed the move. The same laws describe an apple falling from a tree and the Moon moving in its orbit. After Newton, a theory of motion that wasn't mathematical simply couldn't compete. The next two centuries made the language more abstract, and more portable. Lagrange rewrote mechanics so that one method handled many different machines. Fourier described how heat spreads, with differential equations. Now mathematics followed a whole field through space and time, not just a single body. Maxwell's equations united electricity, magnetism and light. Boltzmann showed that laws can be statistical, describing crowds of molecules rather than one trajectory. Then came relativity and quantum mechanics. Gravity became the geometry of spacetime. Particles became wave functions. Mathematics now shaped what physicists could even imagine nature to be. In 1960, Eugene Wigner called this the unreasonable effectiveness of mathematics. Why should equations invented by mathematicians fit the world so well? Philosophers of science added warnings. Karl Popper said a scientific claim must be testable, and it stays a conjecture however well it's supported. Thomas Kuhn showed that the standards of science change during revolutions. Nancy Cartwright argued that many laws work through idealization, and fit the messy world only approximately. So if a computer prints a short equation, what has it found? A pattern in a finite table? An idealized model? A real mechanism? Or our own assumptions, handed back to us? History is clear on one thing. The great equations didn't become great because they were short. They became great because they organized many phenomena, and kept predicting things correctly.

transcript.title: Computers join the search
transcript.text: After the Second World War, computers changed what a law means in practice. An equation could be known, and still its consequences were only reachable by simulation. Then came data intensive science. Telescopes, sensors and simulations started producing more data than anyone could read. And people asked a bolder question. Can a computer propose the equations themselves? Starting in the late 1970s, Pat Langley, Herbert Simon and their colleagues built programs called BACON. Given tables of planetary data, one of them rediscovered Kepler's third law. In the 1990s, genetic programming let computers evolve formulas of any shape. That's where symbolic regression grew up as a method. Later work showed that evolutionary search could recover the laws of moving systems, like pendulums, straight from measured motion. Today, deep learning predicts protein structures, proposes new crystals, and even helps control fusion plasmas. Impressive. But a powerful predictor is not automatically an explanation. Symbolic discovery sits in between. It uses computation to search, but it returns something you can read, test and argue with. An equation.

transcript.title: Prediction is not explanation
transcript.text: Back to the coffee. These measurements come from our own simulation: a cup at ninety degrees, in a twenty degree room, read with a little thermometer noise. The polynomial has five free coefficients. Its typical error on these points is about 0.30 degrees. The exponential has the room temperature built in, plus two numbers: the starting temperature and a rate. Its typical error is about 0.34 degrees. Slightly worse. If predicting these points were the only goal, you'd pick the polynomial and go home. So pause the video for a moment. What do you think each formula predicts after one hour? The exponential settles toward the room. After an hour it says about 20.2 degrees. The polynomial shoots off to almost half a million degrees. The exponential is more than a curve. It says the cup approaches the room temperature, and never passes it. And its rate has units of one over time. It's also the solution of a simple law: the cup cools at a rate proportional to how much warmer it is than the room. That's Newton's law of cooling. The polynomial implies no law at all. It just bends where the data told it to. Here's the standard machine learning recipe. Pick a family of models. Then choose the parameters that make the average loss on your data as small as possible. Notice what's missing. Nothing in that objective asks whether the model matches the process that produced the data. Two models with the same loss count as equally good, even if one respects physics and the other breaks it. That's fine when prediction is the goal. A weather forecast is valuable if it's right tomorrow, even if nobody can read its insides. But if you claim a mechanism, prediction is only one piece of the evidence. So let's separate five modeling goals, from the least demanding to the most demanding. Prediction: estimate outcomes you haven't seen. Explanation: understand why a fitted model behaves the way it does. Careful with that one. Explaining why a neural network made a prediction is not the same as explaining the phenomenon. System identification: recover the structure of a dynamical system, using a vocabulary of terms you chose in advance. Symbolic discovery: search for the equation itself, with its form free to vary. And mechanistic discovery: claim that the equation describes the process that actually produced the data. Each step up asks more of the evidence. Success on one step does not buy you the next. Here's the simplest version of the trap. Measure the sine of x, but only between minus one and one. The polynomial x minus x cubed over six matches it everywhere in that window. The worst miss is less than one hundredth. Now step outside. At x equal to pi, the sine is back at zero. The polynomial says minus two. Inside the window, the two are almost twins. Outside, they disagree completely. Extrapolation exposes the assumptions that interpolation hides. And here's the practical lesson. A hundred more points inside the window tell you almost nothing. A few points where the candidates disagree tell you a lot. For the coffee, a few readings after half an hour beat a hundred more in the first five minutes.

transcript.title: From curve to law
transcript.text: Data alone rarely pin down one explanation. Scientific knowledge does the rest of the work. Units, for example. If x is a length and y is a speed, then y equals x plus x squared adds things that simply can't be added. Symmetry: a law shouldn't depend on where you put the origin of your coordinates. Conservation: some quantities can't appear from nothing. Limits: a formula should behave sensibly when a variable gets very small, or very large. And shape. If a response must rise with pressure, prefer formulas that keep rising, between the data points and beyond them. These aren't checks you run at the very end. The best methods build them into the search itself. Suppose a search returns y equals a x over b plus x. It's compact, and it fits. Now look at the questions it lets you ask. Does y level off as x grows? Must a and b be positive? What units do they carry? Does the mechanism you believe in predict that leveling off? That's the real value of an equation. The algorithm proposed an object to reason about. It didn't finish the reasoning for you. So there's no magic error threshold where a fit becomes a law. Instead, there's a ladder of claims. At the bottom, a formula that predicts the data you have. Then an empirical regularity: it still holds when you repeat the experiment. Then a scientific hypothesis: it respects known constraints and survives a change of regime. Then a mechanism: it beats credible alternatives in experiments designed to tell them apart. And only at the top, a law, within a stated domain. Not at the moment an optimizer first prints an equation. Here's the working definition for this course. Computational symbolic discovery uses search, optimization and scientific constraints to produce explicit equations, as candidate descriptions of a phenomenon. The equation is a hypothesis. Its status depends on evidence beyond the search.

transcript.title: Recap and lab
transcript.text: Let's recap. Mathematics became the language of physics over two thousand years, and computers have now joined the search for equations. Prediction is evidence, not the end point. A curve that fits can still be wrong about the world, and the place to catch it is outside your data. In this module's lab, you'll fit a polynomial and a law to falling ball data, stretch the time window, and watch which one survives. Next video: what symbolic regression actually searches, and why that space is so astonishingly big. See you there.

episodes.title: What symbolic regression searches
episodes.hook: Let the computer choose the shape of a formula, and a friendly fit becomes a search through an astronomically large space.
episodes.takeaway: With four operators and three leaves there are about 1.2 billion formulas with six operators; symbolic regression searches a designed language, so its rules and complexity measure must be reported.

transcript.title: From two numbers to a space of shapes
transcript.text: Fit a straight line to some points. What is the computer actually searching for? Two numbers: a slope and an intercept. That's it. Now let the computer also choose the shape of the formula. Maybe a square, maybe a logarithm, maybe a sine inside a fraction. That one change turns a smooth, friendly problem into a search through an astronomically large space. Today: what symbolic regression searches, how big that space is, and how to search it like a scientist. Three parts. First, what the search space is made of. Second, the workflow that takes us from observations to equations, in seven stages. And third, the properties that make an equation scientifically useful, not just accurate.

transcript.title: What the search space is made of
transcript.text: With a line, y equals a x plus b, the structure is fixed before you look at the data. One multiplication, one addition, two constants. Fitting means moving a and b until the error is smallest. Symbolic regression drops that assumption. Should x appear once, or squared? Should two variables be added, or multiplied? Is there an exponential in there, and what sits inside it? Only after the structure is chosen do the constants get their values. So the expressions themselves become the objects being optimized. One compact way to write the goal: find the formula f, from a language of allowed expressions, that minimizes the error on the data plus lambda times the complexity of f. That language, written as a curly H, is the quiet star of the equation. It's not all of mathematics. It's what you can build from the variables, constants, operators and rules you gave the algorithm. And the problem has two layers. Choosing a structure is discrete: a sine or no sine, a plus or a times. Fitting its constants is continuous. Symbolic regression has to do both, again and again. Computers store a formula as a tree. Take a damped oscillation: c, times e to the minus k t, times the sine of omega t. The leaves hold variables and constants. The inner nodes hold operations. To evaluate it, you work from the leaves up to the root. Now watch the two kinds of moves. Change a constant, and you edit one leaf. Change the structure, and a whole branch is replaced: the sine becomes a cosine, or the exponential disappears. So the search moves through a space of small programs, not over a smooth landscape of parameters. And that space is full of duplicates. x one plus x two, and x two plus x one, are different trees for the same function. x plus x is the same function as two times x. The log of a times b equals the log of a plus the log of b, whenever both are positive. Without care, a search can spend most of its effort rediscovering the same function in different clothes. So how big is this space? Let's count, with a tiny language. Four operators: plus, minus, times and divide. Three possible leaves: x, y, and a constant c. A tree with n operators has n plus one leaves. The number of tree shapes is a Catalan number. Then every operator slot has four choices, and every leaf has three. With one operator, there are 36 formulas. With two, 864. With three, almost 26,000. With six operators, about 1.2 billion. And that's a language with no sine, no exponential, and no second constant. Pause for a second. Allow ten operators. How long would it take to check every formula, at a million formulas per second? There are about 3.1 quadrillion of them. At a million per second, that's roughly ninety nine years. So a real system can't read every formula. It has to decide where to look. Constraints, typing rules and grammars help by removing whole regions before anything is evaluated. Picture an enormous library that you can't read book by book. Each search method is a strategy for choosing the next shelf. Evolutionary methods modify promising formulas and keep useful pieces. Sequential generators write a formula one symbol at a time. Tree search expands promising partial formulas. Neural methods learn, from earlier problems, which constructions tend to be useful. They can reach similar answers by very different routes. But remember this. Search strategy and search space are different things. The best strategy in the world can't find a formula its language can't express. Say the true signal is a sine wave, but your language only has plus, times, variables and constants. The search may return a polynomial that hugs the wave over a short stretch, with a tiny training error. That's not an optimization failure. The right equation was never available to be found. So you add the sine. But every new operator grows the space, and some bring trouble. A logarithm needs positive inputs. Division can blow up. An exponential can overflow. The operator list controls how many invalid and unstable candidates you invite in. A grammar gives finer control. Instead of letting any operator connect to anything, it defines which mathematical sentences are valid. For physics, the grammar can carry units. If v is a speed and t is a time, then v plus t is easy to build, and meaningless. A unit-aware grammar blocks it before it's ever evaluated. Think of units as a type system. Plus needs two arguments with the same units. Times combines them. Taking a time derivative removes one power of time. And this is knowledge working during discovery, not as a cosmetic check afterwards. Vocabulary choices go further. You can hand the search higher-level pieces, like a norm or a dot product, so that rotation-friendly formulas are short instead of deep and clumsy. Constants matter too. With no free constants, the search can't even scale a correct structure. With constants allowed everywhere, it can tune almost anything into a decent fit. Even complexity depends on the language. a plus a plus a is five nodes. Three times a is three nodes, if the number three is allowed. Same function, different measured complexity. That's why a single score, error plus lambda times complexity, is only a starting point. One lambda is one exchange rate between accuracy and simplicity. Here's our own example: thirty noisy points from a straight line, with candidates of growing complexity. A constant misses badly. The line, five nodes, has a validation error of 0.107. Add a sine with a fitted frequency, twelve nodes, and the training error drops. But on fresh data, the error rises to 0.122. A degree eight polynomial does worse still, at 0.149. The formulas that are best for their size form a front, the Pareto front. It keeps the trade-off visible, instead of hiding it inside one number. Here's the uncomfortable consequence. Two researchers can run symbolic regression on the same data, and ask different questions. One allows only arithmetic. Another adds sine, exponential and logarithm. A third forbids anything with inconsistent units. Same data, same loss, different candidates. So the algorithm discovered the equation is an incomplete sentence. Which variables? Which operators and constants? Which rules, which complexity measure, which budget? That's the description of your instrument. These assumptions are called search-space bias. Bias isn't a dirty word here. Discovery is impossible without assumptions. The requirement is to make them visible, and test what they do.

transcript.title: Seven stages from observations to equations
transcript.text: Part two. Symbolic discovery isn't an algorithm that eats a table and returns an equation. It's a workflow, and each step is a scientific decision. Seven stages: the question, the evidence, the language, the prior knowledge, the search, the comparison of candidates, and validation. And validation often sends you back to the start. Stage one, the question. Don't ask which package to run. Ask what mathematical relation would answer your scientific problem. Take measurements of a falling object. One person wants a static relation between speed and height. Another wants a differential equation for acceleration. A third wants a fast surrogate for a simulator. Same data, three different targets. Define the variables operationally. Is v an instant speed estimated from positions, a sensor reading, or an average? And state the scope. A law found at low speed in a lab shouldn't quietly claim to work at any speed. Stage two, the evidence. More data isn't automatically more information. Watch an oscillator thousands of times while it barely moves, and you learn a lot about small swings, and nothing about big ones. A small experiment at several amplitudes can tell nonlinear forces apart. Your data set isn't a neutral input file. It's an experimental representation of the phenomenon. Which regimes you sampled decides which equations you can tell apart. Stages three and four, the language and the knowledge. The language must be broad enough to contain the true mechanism, and narrow enough that the search means something. Knowledge can enter as hard rules, soft penalties, priors, unit types, symmetries, conservation laws, signs, or limits. A velocity equal to a length plus a time can be rejected before any constant is tuned. But priors can be wrong. If you force a response to keep rising because every measurement so far rises, you may forbid the real law, which turns over just outside your data. So test your constraints too. Remove one, soften it, swap it for a plausible alternative. If the discovered equation changes a lot, part of the discovery came from you, not from the data. Stage five, the search. Choosing between a line, an exponential and a saturating curve is discrete. Fitting the constants of the chosen one is continuous. Practical systems switch between the two levels all the time. Stage six, comparing candidates. If one formula has an error of 0.021 with six operators, and another has 0.020 with thirty five, the second is not automatically better. One formula dominates another if it's no worse in error, no worse in complexity, and strictly better in at least one. The formulas nobody dominates form the Pareto front. Keep several of them, and let scientific evidence decide. Stage seven, validation. What counts as enough depends on the claim. A fast surrogate for a simulator may only need good held-out predictions. A proposed physical law needs much more. The best question here is not, does it predict the test set? It's: what would we observe if this equation were wrong? Suppose linear drag and quadratic drag both fit your low speed data. Don't collect more low speed data. Push to higher speeds, where the two laws disagree. The equations just designed your next experiment.

transcript.title: What makes an equation useful
transcript.text: Part three. What makes an equation scientifically useful? Here's a checklist, and no single item is enough on its own. Predictive adequacy: does it reproduce held-out data? Parsimony: is it compact enough to inspect? Dimensional consistency: do the units of every term agree? Invariance: does it respect known symmetries? Structural stability: does the same structure come back when you resample? Extrapolation: is it believable outside the fitting range? Identifiability: can your data tell it apart from its rivals? Falsifiability: can it generate a test that could prove it wrong? Even prediction needs care. Say you recorded twelve trajectories, with five hundred time points each. Split the rows at random, and the test set is full of near neighbors of training points. The error looks great, and proves little. If you claim the law works for new trajectories, hold out whole trajectories: train on ten, and test on the other two. The split should mirror the claim. Parsimony is subtle too. A short tree can hide wild behavior, and a longer polynomial with meaningful coefficients can be easier to interpret. Simplicity is relative to how the formula will be used. Units give a sharper test. A real law shouldn't care whether you measured in meters or centimeters. If converting the units breaks the formula, it captured your data format, not the system. And identifiability ties discovery to experiment design. Near zero, the sine and x minus x cubed over six are almost the same. No algorithm can separate them with data from that neighborhood. Only new measurements can. Finally, exact recovery, a favorite benchmark. Did the algorithm find the very formula that generated the data? Sometimes that test is too strict. Two times the sine of x times the cosine of x is just the sine of two x, even though the strings differ. And sometimes it's too lenient. A model trained on millions of formulas, or a language model that has read about the law, may be recalling it rather than inferring it from the numbers. So record provenance. Say the result is: a pendulum's period equals two pi times the square root of L over g. Did the search find the square root and the two pi on its own? Did dimensional analysis leave only one constant to fit? Or was the structure supplied from mechanics? Same final equation, very different discoveries.

transcript.title: Recap
transcript.text: Let's recap. Symbolic regression searches a designed space of small programs, and that space explodes as formulas grow. The language, the constraints and the complexity measure are scientific decisions, so describe them like an instrument. Treat discovery as a seven stage loop, and judge equations by a whole checklist, including provenance. Next video, we put it all to work: a ball falling with unknown drag. And then the failure modes that look exactly like discoveries. See you there.

episodes.title: Falling with unknown drag, and false discoveries
episodes.hook: A ball falls, a sensor logs its speed. Is the drag linear or quadratic, and how do we find out honestly?
episodes.takeaway: Both drag laws fit the first half second; three seconds in, linear says 19.1 m/s and quadratic 9.1, and the data say 9.0. Measure where candidates disagree, and attack your own equations.

transcript.title: A ball, a sensor, a question
transcript.text: A light ball is dropped. A sensor logs its speed fifty times a second. Is the air slowing it down? And if so, how? Today we answer that question properly, the way a careful discovery system should. Then we'll look at the many ways an equation can look like a discovery, and still be wrong. Four parts: the worked example, failure modes, the move toward hybrid discovery systems, and finally, a ladder of five levels for the claims we make about an equation.

transcript.title: Worked example: falling with unknown drag
transcript.text: The setup. The ball falls a short distance, so gravity, g, is constant. We count downward as positive, so the speed v is positive while it falls. Three classic candidates. Free fall: the acceleration is just g. Linear drag: g minus k one times v. Quadratic drag: g minus k two times v times the absolute value of v. While the ball falls, v times its absolute value is just v squared. The absolute value keeps the drag pointing against the motion, if the ball ever moves up. But we don't want to just pick the best of three. We want a broader family of formulas to compete, with enough physics built in that the search doesn't waste time on nonsense. The first information arrives before any fitting: units. Speed is length over time. Acceleration and g are length over time squared. Every term added to g must also be an acceleration. So k one must have units of one over time, and k two must have units of one over length. That already removes candidates. g minus v squared is inadmissible, because v squared is length squared over time squared. It only becomes legal with a coefficient measured per meter. And it tells us what our numbers mean. A coefficient of 0.12 in front of v squared is really 0.12 per meter. Change units, and the number changes, but the physics must not. Next decision: what did we actually measure? Position and speed. Not acceleration. So one option is to estimate acceleration from neighboring speed readings, by finite differences. In our simulation, the sensor's noise is just five centimeters per second. But we divide a difference of two noisy readings by two hundredths of a second. The result: the estimated acceleration is off by about 4.3 meters per second squared, on a typical reading. That's almost half of g. Fit a polynomial in v to those noisy accelerations, and you get a positive v squared term. Drag that pushes the ball faster. The algorithm is explaining differentiation noise, not motion. The alternative: don't fit the derivative at all. Take each candidate law, integrate it forward from the measured starting speed, and compare the whole trajectory with the data. Same experiment, a different way of scoring, and the ranking of candidates can change. Preprocessing is part of the discovery procedure. Report it like the algorithm itself. Now the language: plus, minus, times, divide, and the absolute value. The leaves are v, g, and free constants, whose units are worked out as the tree is built. And four rules. One: the right side must be an acceleration. Two: it must be real for every speed we can see. Three: drag never pushes the ball forward. Four: as the speed goes to zero, the acceleration goes to g. Each rule removes a different kind of nonsense. Rule three kills g plus k v. Rule four kills a constant hanging around at zero speed. These rules describe this experiment, not every falling object. Add buoyancy, or a propeller, and they can break. If the assumptions change, change the search space, and search again. Experiment one: half a second after release, twenty six speed readings, with noise of 0.05 meters per second. Free fall misses: its typical error is 0.18, more than three times the noise. Gravity alone can't explain the data. Linear drag fits with k one equal to 0.314 per second, and a typical error of 0.068. Quadratic drag fits with k two equal to 0.119 per meter, and an error of 0.061. Both curves run straight through the cloud of points. The difference between them is a fraction of the sensor noise. And the mixed candidate, with both terms? Under the rule that drag can't push forward, its linear part went all the way to zero. It became the quadratic law. Pause here. Linear and quadratic both fit the first half second. What does each predict three seconds after release? Linear drag says 19.1 meters per second, still rising toward a terminal speed of about 31. Quadratic drag says 9.1, already settled at its terminal speed. Two equations that were nearly identical in the experiment disagree by a factor of two, just a few seconds later. So we run experiment two. Same ball, dropped from higher, measured for three full seconds. The data settle at 9.0 meters per second. Quadratic drag's typical error over the whole fall is 0.057. Linear drag's is 5.1. Linear drag is out. And where should we have looked? The two laws drift apart by more than three times the noise after just 0.58 seconds. The most informative measurement was just past where we stopped. That's the general recipe. Measure where the candidates disagree by much more than your noise. Don't densely resample the region where they agree. Now repeat with a second, lighter ball. Quadratic drag fits again, but now k two is 0.19 per meter. That doesn't contradict the law. It tells us k two depends on things that were fixed in the first experiment: the air's density, the ball's size, its mass. So the discovered constant becomes the target of a new search: k two as a function of density, area and mass. Notice the separate claims. A formula that predicts this fall is an empirical result. The same structure across experiments is a structural result. A coefficient that follows the ball's properties points toward a mechanism. None of that follows from having the smallest error.

transcript.title: Failure modes that look like discoveries
transcript.text: Part two: failure modes that look like discoveries. An equation carries authority. You can print it, simplify it, plot it. And many failures don't look like failures. They come with low error, stable-looking constants and elegant formulas. Failure one: a narrow operating range. The truth is the sine of x, but you only measured x from −0.3 up to +0.3. There, y equals x is wrong by less than five thousandths. At x equal to pi it predicts 3.14, and the truth is zero. Several different laws looked identical, because the experiment never visited the place where they differ. Failure two: noisy derivatives. You saw it with the ball: the fit to noisy accelerations invented a v squared term that pushes the ball forward. Extra terms like that can look statistically justified, and even physically suggestive. Now integrate that polynomial forward. It levels off at about 6.2 meters per second, while the ball really reaches 9. The plain quadratic law tracks the whole fall. The extras were modeling the noise of differentiation. Failure three: a missing variable. Say a plant's growth rate is really controlled by light, but you didn't record light. You recorded temperature, which rose with the light every day. The search finds a neat power law in temperature. It fits beautifully. Repeated runs even agree on the exponent. Then someone heats the greenhouse at night, and the law vanishes. It was a faithful summary of a correlation, interpreted as a mechanism. No search budget can recover a variable you never measured. The same happens in dynamics. Hide one variable of a simple linear system, and a formula in the visible variable alone sprouts squared and cubed terms to make up for it. Failure four: too many operators. Remember our noisy straight line. With a sine available, the search added a small wiggle with a frequency of about 33. Draw a fresh noisy sample, and the line part barely changes, but the wiggle's frequency jumps to about 45. The part that survives the resample is the part worth keeping. So overfitting in symbolic regression doesn't always look like a giant polynomial. It can hide inside one short, powerful operator. A formula can look simple and be statistically complex. And the opposite mistake exists too. Push simplicity too hard, and a real but modest cubic term gets erased. Parsimony is a preference, not a proof. Failure five: priors that become prejudice. Forbid any term that grows with time, because you expect a steady state, and a slow drift can never be found. The fit then confirms the steady state, which was never allowed to fail. Failure six: unit leakage. Standardize x, find y equals 2.6 times the standardized x, plus 0.35, and those constants describe your preprocessing, not the physics. Add standardized time to standardized length, and nothing complains. Failure seven: memorization. A pretrained model sees data from Newton's law of gravitation and returns it instantly. Perfect recovery? Or did it read about that law during training? That's not cheating, scientists use prior knowledge too. But the claim changes. It's prior knowledge combined with data, not discovery from data alone. Blinded targets and new formulas test the difference. Failure eight: reporting the best run. Run a randomized search fifty times. If the exact law appears twice, the method makes the discovery possible, not reliable. A method with one brilliant run and a poor median can look better than a method that's good every single time. Report distributions: of errors, of structures, of coefficients. In real projects these failures stack. A short range hides a missing variable. Noisy derivatives feed an over-rich language. A strong prior makes the invented terms look meaningful. And the luckiest run gets the paper. The answer is not to distrust symbolic discovery. It's to attack surprising equations on purpose. Change the regime. Repeat the experiment. Change the preprocessing. Soften the priors. Hold out whole trajectories. Rerun the search. Add plausible missing variables. Change the units. A false discovery is often convincing only because nobody ran the experiment that would make it fail.

transcript.title: Toward hybrid discovery systems
transcript.text: Part three. The newest change in the field isn't one algorithm. It's a change in the unit of design: from an optimizer that returns an equation, to a discovery system. In such a system, symbolic regression may be just one stage. It turns numbers into an explicit hypothesis, or compresses what another model learned, or proposes a missing term in a mechanistic model. Language models write candidate equations as programs, run them, and revise them. Other systems, like AI Hilbert, demand that a formula be consistent with the data and derivable from background theory at the same time. Some systems span much more of research. The AI Scientist runs a computational research loop, from ideas and code to experiments and drafted papers. Coscientist connects a language model planner to documentation, code and automated lab equipment. The A-Lab runs materials synthesis in a closed loop, learning from failed attempts. But optimization asks where the best point is. Discovery asks what the observations teach us about the system. The second one is the hard one. And humans don't disappear. A scientist notices an anomaly, adds a variable no instrument recorded, spots an instrument artifact, or decides the whole question was wrong. There's also a risk: fluent outputs can create an illusion of understanding. Judge a hybrid system by whether it makes assumptions and uncertainty easier to inspect, not just by how much it automates. And label outputs honestly. An equation distilled from a neural network, retrieved by a language model, fitted to synthetic data, or recovered from new measurements, has a different evidential status. Don't call them all laws.

transcript.title: A ladder of five claims
transcript.text: Which brings us to the last part: a ladder of five levels for what an equation means. Each level keeps the demands of the one below, and adds a new one. Level one: a predictive symbolic model. It predicts held-out data from the same experiment. Like a polynomial for the first five minutes of a cooling cup. Useful, but repeat the experiment and the formula may change. Level two: a robust empirical relation. It comes back under resampling, new runs and new data sets, over a stated range. Like a pump's flow versus speed curve that holds across several test runs. Level three: a physically admissible relation. It also respects units, symmetries, signs and limits. Linear drag can reach this level: the right units, drag against the motion, and g at zero speed. But if your experiment never reached speeds where quadratic drag looks different, admissible is all you can say. Not yet a mechanism. Level four: a candidate mechanism. It has beaten credible rivals in a discriminating experiment. Our high speed drop did that for quadratic drag. Showing that k two changes with the ball's area would strengthen it further. Level five: a supported scientific law, within a stated domain. Independent experiments, theory and replication all agree. Ohm's law for an ordinary resistor, inside its working range, is a classic example. And the domain is part of the claim, not an embarrassment added later. Heat the resistor too much and the law bends. That doesn't make it wrong. It makes it a law with a domain. Symbolic regression can climb the first levels in seconds. The top levels need something different in kind: rival mechanisms, new experiments, and evidence from beyond the search that proposed the equation.

transcript.title: Module 1 recap
transcript.text: That wraps up Module one. Units first. Fit trajectories, not noisy derivatives. Measure where the candidates disagree. Attack your own discoveries. And use the ladder to say exactly how far an equation has climbed. In the lab, you'll fit polynomial and drag laws to falling ball data, stretch the window, and see which one survives. There's a Kepler variant too, with one planet held out. Next module: the mathematical languages we use to write symbolic models. Trees, grammars, constants and complexity. See you there.

episodes.title: Expressions as computational objects
episodes.hook: One formula, six objects: a computer never searches mathematics itself, only the language someone chose.
episodes.takeaway: With six operators, our tiny language has about 8.9 billion formulas and fewer than 4% pass the unit check; units are a filter, not a validation.

transcript.title: One formula, six objects
transcript.text: Here's one formula: a cup cooling in a room, with a small heater switching on and off. c times the room temperature minus T, plus q times the sine of omega t. Now here it is again, five more times. As a tree. As prefix and postfix strings. As a graph. And as a derivation from a grammar. Which one is the formula? All of them, and none of them. A computer never searches mathematics itself. It searches one of these objects, and each object changes what the search can see, reach and break. Welcome to Module two. This video has three parts: a short history of mathematical notation, the main ways a computer stores a formula, and grammars with units, the rules that decide which sentences are allowed.

transcript.title: From words to symbols
transcript.text: Before equations, there were marks: notches on a stick, tokens for grain, counts of animals and days. Algebra itself is older than its symbols. For centuries, problems were solved in words. Symbols arrived slowly. In 1557, Robert Recorde introduced the equals sign: two parallel lines, because no two things could be more equal. Around 1591, François Viète used letters for both known and unknown quantities, so whole families of problems could share one form. In 1637, Descartes tied algebra to curves. Calculus made change itself writable. Leibniz published his notation for differentials in 1684, and Newton wrote about fluxions, quantities flowing in time. Now the unknown could be a whole trajectory, not a number. The idea of a function grew too. Euler treated functions as analytic expressions. Later, mathematicians accepted any rule that gives each input one output, with or without a formula. So a formula, a table, a graph and a program can carry the same mathematical content, and still be different objects. In the 1930s, Church and Turing made computation itself mathematical: symbols manipulated by finite rules. That's the bridge to us. An expression tree, a token sequence, a grammar: each is a modern encoding of choices that mathematicians made over centuries. A symbolic regression system never searches mathematics in general. It searches a language that someone chose.

transcript.title: What an expression language is
transcript.text: So what is an expression language? It's the primitive symbols, the rules for combining them, the type or unit rules, and the way candidates are stored. It defines the hypothesis space before any optimization begins. If the language has multiplication but no powers, a power law is still expressible, but only as a long product. If it allows unrestricted division and logarithms, it contains short formulas that break on part of your data. A language is an inductive bias. It changes how likely a useful equation is to be short, reachable and valid. Often it matters as much as the search algorithm.

transcript.title: Formulas as computational objects
transcript.text: Part two: formulas as computational objects. Start with the tree. For our heater formula, the root is a plus. On one side, c times the room temperature minus T. On the other, q times the sine of omega t. The tree makes dependencies explicit: to evaluate the root, first evaluate its children. Depth measures nesting. Node count gives one notion of size. And any subtree is a complete piece that can be cut out and replaced. Now mutate one branch. Replace the sine of omega t by omega t squared. One small edit in the tree. But a bounded wiggle has become a term that grows without limit. Computational distance and mathematical distance are different things. Two trees one edit apart can behave completely differently, and two very different trees can be the same function. The search moves through a geometry made by the representation. A tree can also be flattened. Take x minus two, times y. In prefix form, each operator comes first: times, minus, x, two, y. In postfix form, it comes last: x, two, minus, y, times. No parentheses are needed, as long as you know how many arguments each operator takes. Prefix strings are great for generators. Write plus, sine, x. The sine is complete, but the plus still has one open slot. Keep counting open slots, and when the count reaches zero, the formula is done. If it can't reach zero within the length limit, reject it early. Flat sequences store compactly, hash quickly and evaluate fast, which matters when you test millions of candidates. But edits get harder. A subtree becomes an interval that you can only find by counting arguments. And swapping a sine for a plus suddenly demands an extra argument, so the rest of the string has to be repaired or rejected. And remember, well formed is not meaningful. The log of minus three is a perfectly formed string. So is x divided by x minus x. Both are valid syntax, and useless. Tree-based genetic programming loves a property called closure. Every operator accepts whatever the others return, so any subtree can be attached anywhere. That's convenient: variation rarely creates broken formulas. Science often wants less freedom. A vector shouldn't go where a number belongs. Seconds shouldn't be added to meters. And the logarithm of a length makes no sense. Types and units bring those distinctions back. Trees also repeat themselves. In e to the minus t, times the cosine of t, plus e to the minus t, the exponential appears twice. A tree stores both copies: ten nodes. A graph with sharing stores it once: six nodes. Sharing changes mutation too. Change the shared node, and both uses change at once. Copy it first, and the two uses drift apart. The same nominal move does different mathematics. It even changes what complexity means. Count stored nodes, and you measure computing cost. Count visible symbols, and you measure what a reader has to parse. Neural generators use yet another object: a sequence of tokens, usually in prefix order. A transformer writes a formula symbol by symbol, like a sentence, and a parser turns it back into a tree. Validity and equivalence then need explicit care: masks that forbid impossible next tokens, and checks that catch the same formula written twice.

transcript.title: Grammars and units
transcript.text: Part three: grammars. A list of operators says what exists. A grammar says where it may appear. Here's a small grammar of our own. An expression is a sum of terms. A term is a product of factors. A factor is x, a constant, or e to the power of minus a constant times x. This grammar can't build the exponential of an exponential, or the exponential of x plus one. It allows decay terms under the exponential, and nothing else. The grammar has quietly encoded a physical expectation. Here's a question for you. Two grammars produce exactly the same set of formulas. Can they still lead to different discoveries? Pause and think. They can. We generated random formulas from one language with two sets of production weights. With the sine chosen five percent of the time, about thirty one percent of the formulas contained a sine. At twenty percent, sixty one percent did. Same language, same reachable formulas, very different search. Under a finite budget, whatever is easy to say gets said more often. Some methods go one step further, as in grammatical evolution: they evolve a code of numbers, and the grammar decodes it into a formula. The object being varied and the formula you read are now different things. One changed number can redirect a whole derivation and rewrite an entire subtree. And many different codes can decode to the same formula. Syntax alone happily builds x plus t. To catch that, attach units to every expression: the powers of length and of time that it carries. Multiply, and the powers add. Divide, and they subtract. Add or subtract, and they must match. Exponentials, logarithms and sines need a pure number inside. Now bad formulas are rejected while they're being built. They never get evaluated, and never enter the population. How much does that remove? We counted a tiny language: plus, minus, times and divide, with four leaves: a length x, a time t, a speed v, and a pure number c. With two operators there are 2,048 formulas, and only 744 pass the unit check. With four operators there are about 3.7 million, and about 430,000 pass, roughly twelve percent. With six operators, about 8.9 billion formulas, and fewer than four percent survive. Require the answer to be a speed, and only about a quarter of one percent remain. That's not only a speed up. The search spends its effort on formulas that could mean something. But a valid formula can still be wrong. Units don't prove causality, conservation, or the right behavior at the extremes. Units are a filter, not a validation.

transcript.title: Recap
transcript.text: Let's recap. A formula on paper becomes a computational object: a tree, a flat sequence, a graph, a token stream, or a grammar derivation. Each one decides what is close, what is valid, and what is cheap. Grammars and units decide which sentences can even be written. They are scientific assumptions, so write them down. In this module's lab, you'll build trees, see their prefix and postfix forms, mutate branches, and count how many formulas survive the unit rules. Next video: constants, equivalence, and why complexity depends on your language.

episodes.title: Constants, equivalence and complexity
episodes.hook: A search returns 6.296. Is that 2π, or just a number that happened to fit?
episodes.takeaway: Least squares reached the noise level in 6 evaluations where 1,000 random guesses did not; and the bell curve is simpler than a quadratic by node count, more complex by depth, and tied by weight.

transcript.title: Is 6.296 really 2π?
transcript.text: A search returns a constant: 6.296. Is that two pi? Or just a number that happened to fit? Today: the numbers inside formulas, the many disguises of a single formula, and why simple depends on who is counting. At the end, we'll design a language for a pendulum, before touching any data.

transcript.title: Constants: the continuous unknowns
transcript.text: Part one: constants. A formula has two kinds of unknowns. Its structure is discrete. Its constants are continuous. Take y equals a times x over b plus x, a curve that rises and levels off. Once that shape is chosen, finding a and b is ordinary curve fitting. Searching for them with the same machinery that searches structure is usually a waste. Here's our example: twenty five simulated noisy points from that curve. The true values are 2.5 for a, and 0.8 for b. Strategy one: guess random constants. With ten guesses, the best typical error is 0.21. With a hundred guesses, 0.10. With a thousand guesses, 0.062. Strategy two: nonlinear least squares, starting from one and one. Six evaluations later, the error is 0.031, right at the noise level. It finds a at 2.47, and b at 0.74. Between these extremes there's a whole menu. A small fixed set of numbers, like one, two and pi. Linear least squares, when the constants enter linearly. Gradient methods, through formulas that can be differentiated. Or neural networks that predict constants from the data, followed by polishing. Each has a weakness. A fixed set can't fit arbitrary scales. Local methods depend on where they start. And predicted constants usually need refinement. Constants can also be redundant. Write the same curve as c one times c two times x, over b plus x. Now one times 2.47 gives exactly the same fit as two times 1.23. So does five times 0.49. The data can only pin down the product. Redundant constants create flat valleys, slow down the optimizer, and produce numbers that mean nothing on their own. Then comes the tempting question: is a fitted constant secretly famous? We simulated a pendulum at eight lengths, with a hundredth of a second of timing noise, and fitted T equals c times the square root of L over g. The fit gives c equal to 6.296, give or take 0.013. Two pi is 6.283, within about one standard error. So two pi is consistent with the data. But so are many nearby numbers. Replacing the fit by two pi is a claim. Show the evidence, or keep the fitted number.

transcript.title: Equivalence: one formula, many disguises
transcript.text: Part two: equivalence. Symbolic spaces are full of disguises. x plus x, two times x, and x times one plus one are the same function, and three different trees. x squared minus one, over x minus one, equals x plus one everywhere except at one, where the first is undefined. And the square root of x squared is the absolute value of x, not x. So same equation needs a definition. Here are four levels of sameness. Syntactic: the same string. Algebraic: one can be rewritten into the other by accepted rules. Numerical: the same values, within a tolerance, on the domain you care about. And scientific: the same predictions that matter for the application, including limits, symmetries, and what happens under an intervention. How much redundancy is out there? We grew ten thousand random trees, up to depth three, from plus, minus, times, x, one and two. There were 6,298 different trees. But evaluated at a few points, they formed only 872 different functions. And a single function made up twelve percent of everything we drew. Tools fight this. A canonicalizer rewrites formulas into one standard form: sort the arguments of plus and times, collect the numbers, drop times one and plus zero. Hashing finds identical subtrees fast. Equality graphs, or e-graphs for short, store many equivalent forms at once, so a search can recognize a formula it has already seen in another costume. But simplification carries assumptions. Rewriting e to the log of x as x assumes x is positive. Cancelling x over x assumes x is never zero, and a pendulum passes through zero twice in every swing. And computers don't do exact arithmetic. Add one to ten to the sixteen, then subtract ten to the sixteen, and you get zero. Do the subtraction first, then add one, and you get one. Same algebra, different answer.

transcript.title: Complexity depends on the language
transcript.text: Part three: complexity. Model selection trades error against complexity. But what is complexity, exactly? Node count is easy, but it treats a sine like a plus. Depth measures nesting. Weighted counts charge more for exponentials and powers. Description length asks how many bits it takes to write the formula down. Other measures count nonlinearity, or the cost of evaluating, or how hard the formula is for a person to use. Quick test. Which is simpler: a x squared plus b x plus c, or a times e to the minus b x squared? Pause and decide. By node count, the bell curve wins: nine nodes against eleven. By depth, the polynomial wins: four levels against five. And with heavier weights for exponentials and powers, they tie at thirteen. We ranked six common formulas under three measures. The line and the power law stay simplest under all three. The logistic curve is fifth by node count, but last by depth and by weighted cost. So declare your complexity measure before you see the results. Otherwise it's far too easy to pick the measure that flatters your favorite. Representation also shapes the search itself. Small edits can cause big changes. Big edits can change nothing. And trees can keep growing without improving the fit, a problem called bloat. Some methods vary formulas by their behavior instead of their syntax. Others choose parents one data case at a time, which keeps specialists alive. Each changes which formulas survive long enough to matter.

transcript.title: Designing a language for a pendulum
transcript.text: Part four: let's design a language before touching any data. A pendulum swings with air drag. We measure the angle theta and the angular speed omega, and we want a law for the angular acceleration. Units first. The angle is a pure number. Omega has units of one over time. The target has units of one over time squared. A conservative language: plus, minus, times, and the sine of the angle, which is allowed because the angle is a pure number. It already contains the classic law: minus c one times the sine of theta, minus c two times omega. And the units assign every constant a physical type. c one must carry one over time squared. c two must carry one over time. A broader language adds absolute value and division. Now minus c three times omega times the absolute value of omega becomes reachable: air drag that grows with the square of the speed. Here c three turns out to be a pure number. That's more expressive, but the space is bigger, and division brings new questions about dividing by zero. Broader is justified only when your question needs those alternatives. Before searching, also declare the equivalence policy. Sort commutative arguments, collect constants, drop zeros and ones. And never cancel omega over omega, because omega is zero at every turning point. Declare the complexity weights now as well, not after you've seen the winners. Here's the checklist to write down before any run: the terminals, the operators with their arities and domains, the unit rules, the constant strategy, the size limits, the simplification and equivalence rules, the complexity measure, and any special building blocks. Report it like an apparatus. It matters as much as the optimizer's settings. So which representation should you choose? Trees are a strong default for compact laws in a few variables. Graphs help when pieces repeat. Grammars help when you know the roles of terms. Token sequences suit neural generators. And fixed libraries of terms suit problems where you already know the vocabulary. No representation is best for everything. Choose the one that exposes the structure your question is about.

transcript.title: Recap
transcript.text: Let's recap. Constants are continuous: fit them numerically, watch for redundancy, and snap them to famous numbers only with evidence. Equivalent formulas waste search unless you define sameness and remove duplicates carefully. And complexity depends on the language, so fix your measure in advance. In the lab, you'll test equivalence at random points, compare complexity measures, and design your own language. Next module: encoding physics and domain knowledge. See you there.

episodes.title: Knowledge you can execute
episodes.hook: A cubic fits a draining tank to within two millimetres, then predicts a level of minus 17 cm. We knew better; the search didn't.
episodes.takeaway: A soft never-rises rule repaired the cubic's three-minute prediction (from −17 cm to about 6 cm) at no cost inside the data; units turned five variables into three groups, and forty runs collapsed onto one line.

transcript.title: A tank, a cubic, and an impossible level
transcript.text: A tank drains through a small hole. We log its water level every two seconds, for one minute. Two formulas fit that minute equally well, to within two millimetres: a cubic polynomial, and Torricelli's law with two constants. Now ask them about the future. After three minutes, the cubic says the level is minus 17 centimetres. Torricelli says 6. The tank empties after about five minutes. We knew all along that water can't go below empty. The search didn't, because nobody told it in a form it could execute. Welcome to Module three: encoding physics and domain knowledge. In this video: the kinds of knowledge we have, four ways to inject the same knowledge, and units, the most executable knowledge of all, right up to dimensionless groups. Here's the principle for this module. Scientific discovery is data evidence, plus search, plus explicit knowledge, plus independent tests. It's not an equation you can solve. It's a reminder that knowledge can enter at many points, and that the same knowledge can enter in more than one way. A scientific constraint is a computable restriction, preference or test that comes from what we already know. If it doesn't change which formulas are generated, kept or trusted, it isn't doing any work.

transcript.title: Kinds of knowledge
transcript.text: Part one: what kinds of knowledge are there? Let's sort them, using our tank. Units: the level is a length, so the speed of the water leaving the hole must be a length per time. Conservation: the water that leaves through the hole is exactly the water missing from the tank. Symmetry: turn the tank around its axis, and nothing changes. Shape: with no inflow, the level never rises, and it never goes below empty. Boundary and initial knowledge: at the start, the level is 40 centimetres. Asymptotic knowledge: as the tank nearly empties, the outflow shrinks toward zero. A mechanistic skeleton: the level falls at a rate set by the outflow, and only the outflow law is unknown. And finally, hypotheses from experts or the literature: Torricelli's law suggests a square root. Eight kinds of knowledge, and they're mathematically different objects. Lump them all into one penalty, and later you can't tell which one did the work. Two more distinctions help. Some knowledge is universal: any physical equation must be dimensionally consistent. Some is specific to one system and one regime: this tank, this range of levels. And some knowledge restricts the form of an equation, like no logarithm of a length. Other knowledge restricts its behaviour, like a level that never rises.

transcript.title: One rule, four ways to use it
transcript.text: Part two: one piece of knowledge, four ways to use it. Take the rule: the level never rises, and never goes below empty. Hard: candidates that break the rule are rejected, or can't even be built. Soft: breaking it adds a penalty to the score. Preferential: the rule tilts which candidates get proposed or ranked first, with no guarantee. Post-hoc: search first, and throw away the violators at the end. Hard gives the most consistency, but locks out the truth if the knowledge is wrong. Soft tolerates approximate knowledge, but needs a weight. Post-hoc is easy, and wastes effort on hopeless regions. Let's try the soft version on our cubic. We add a penalty for any rise, and for any level below zero, over the next four minutes. Even a tiny weight changes the picture. Inside the minute of data, the fit is just as good: still within two millimetres. But after three minutes, the cubic now says about 6 centimetres, close to Torricelli. Knowledge that agrees with the data costs almost nothing where the data are, and repairs the predictions where they aren't. Here's a question. Should every piece of knowledge become a hard rule? Pause and think about what could go wrong. It depends on how sure you are. A useful order of confidence: mathematical necessity, then well established physical principles, then theory for one regime, then empirical regularities, then expert hunches, and last, suggestions from a machine. Adding seconds to metres is structurally wrong, so a hard rule is safe. A trend seen only in your measured range deserves a soft or range-limited check. A constraint suggested by a language model deserves even less authority. Match the mode to the confidence, and write down which is which. Knowledge can also act at different moments: while a formula is being built, while it's scored, or when the finished formulas are screened. Building-time rules are the cheapest: an invalid branch is cut before anything is evaluated. Scoring-time rules can keep fit and plausibility as separate objectives, and show the trade-off as a Pareto front.

transcript.title: Units as executable knowledge
transcript.text: Part three: units, the most executable knowledge of all. Write each quantity's dimensions as a vector of powers of mass, length and time. A water level is zero, one, zero. A flow rate, volume per time, is zero, three, minus one. Gravity's acceleration is zero, one, minus two. Multiplying adds the vectors. Dividing subtracts them. Adding requires them to be equal. And functions like the sine and the exponential need the zero vector inside. Units become a type system that runs at every node. Checked while a tree is being built, a unit rule stops invalid branches before they cost a single evaluation.

transcript.title: Dimensionless groups
transcript.text: But units can do more than reject formulas. They can shrink the problem itself. The drain time of our tank depends on four quantities: the starting level h, gravity g, the hole area a, and the tank area A. Together with the time T, that's five, built from two base dimensions, length and time. Put their exponents in a two by five matrix. Any product of powers whose exponents lie in the matrix's null space has no units at all. Five quantities, rank two, so three independent dimensionless groups. One choice: T times the square root of g over h. The area ratio, a over A. And A over h squared. So the law must say: the first group equals some function of the other two. Three variables instead of five, before we've seen any data. Let's test it. We simulated forty drain experiments with different levels, holes and tanks, with two percent timing noise. Plotted raw, drain time against starting level, the points scatter everywhere. Plotted as the first group against the area ratio, on log scales, they fall onto one line. Its slope is minus 1.00. Its constant is 2.31, and Torricelli's law with our discharge coefficient gives 2.36. The third group turns out not to matter at all. Units told us which variables to combine. The data told us the shape of the function. The choice of groups isn't unique. T squared times g over h is just as dimensionless. Equivalent groups can make the search easier or harder, so choosing them is a modeling decision, not paperwork. And beware of a look-alike. Subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation makes a number unitless, but not physically dimensionless. Its meaning depends on the centre and the scale you chose. A law found in standardized variables has to be transformed back before you read any physics into it.

transcript.title: Recap
transcript.text: Let's recap. Knowledge comes in kinds: units, conservation, symmetry, shape, boundary values, limits, skeletons and hypotheses. Each can enter as a hard rule, a soft penalty, a preference, or a final screen. Match the mode to your confidence. Units are the most executable knowledge: they type-check every node, and dimensional analysis can turn five variables into three groups before you collect any data.
