In this module's lab, you'll tag variables with units, watch candidates get rejected, find dimensionless groups, and slide between hard and soft rules. Next video: conservation, symmetry, shape, and partial models.

episodes.title: Conservation, symmetry, shape and partial models
episodes.hook: Forty small tanks, one big question: climb a ladder of knowledge and measure what each rung buys.
episodes.takeaway: On ten big tanks, data alone missed by 174% (eight negative drain times); units brought it to 1.8% and the scaling rung to 1.5% with Cd = 0.600. A wrong prior kept the error near 58% at every weight.

transcript.title: Forty small tanks, one big question
transcript.text: Forty small tanks, drained and timed. Now predict a big one: two metres of water, a hole two centimetres wide. How much should you trust your formula? We'll climb a ladder of knowledge one rung at a time, and measure what each rung buys. On the way up: conservation, symmetry, shape, limits, partial models, and what happens when the knowledge is wrong.

transcript.title: Conservation and balance
transcript.text: Part one: conservation. Many laws say that something changes only through flows in and out, and through sources and sinks. For the tank, the rate of change of the water volume equals the inflow minus the outflow. Spread over space and time, the same idea becomes a density, a flux, and a source. Written for a whole region, a balance lets you integrate instead of differentiate. And with noisy data, integrating is gentle, while differentiating amplifies the noise. Let's measure that. Seventy six level readings, one every two seconds, with two millimetres of noise. We want the outflow law: the level falls at a rate proportional to h to some power p. The truth is one half. Estimate the slope at each reading by finite differences, then fit: p comes out 0.55. Fit whole simulated level curves instead: p comes out 0.496. The discharge coefficient comes out 0.59; the true value is 0.6. Same data, same law. Integrating the model beat differentiating the data. Conservation can be a penalty on a residual, or it can be built into the form, so that a violation can't even be written. When a property is exact, building it in usually beats punishing it again and again. Sometimes you only know that something is conserved, not what. Take a frictionless pendulum. Is there a combination of the angular speed squared and the cosine of the angle that stays constant? We searched for the constant c in omega squared plus c times cosine theta that varies least along four simulated swings. The best value is minus 19.6. Twice g over the length is 19.62. That's energy, found from trajectories alone.

transcript.title: Symmetry and coordinates
transcript.text: Part two: symmetry. A symmetry says that changing the description shouldn't change the law. For a scalar, like a potential energy, invariance means the value doesn't change when you rotate the coordinates. For a vector, like a force, equivariance means it rotates right along with them. The cheapest encoding is invariant variables. A central potential written in x and y is k over the square root of x squared plus y squared: ten nodes. Written in the distance r, it's k over r: three nodes. Choose coordinates in which the law is simple, and the search gets easier for free. Real systems are rarely perfectly symmetric. A tilted table, a draft, an uneven wall can break the ideal. So instead of deleting every candidate that breaks the symmetry, score how much it breaks it, or allow a small symmetry-breaking term, and let the data decide whether it's needed. Ask not only which expression fits, but in which coordinates the law becomes simple.

transcript.title: Shape, boundaries, limits and skeletons
transcript.text: Part three: shape. Often you know less than a mechanism, but more than nothing: a sign, a trend, a curvature, a bound, a saturation, a period. For our tank: the outflow grows with the level, and grows ever more slowly. We fitted a quartic to outflow measured between ten and forty centimetres. A counterexample search over the declared range, zero to one metre, finds the first violation at 33 centimetres, still inside the data: there the quartic starts bending upward. At one metre it predicts 970 cubic centimetres per second. The truth is 134. Store every shape constraint with the range where you believe it, and how sure you are. A constraint without a range is stronger than you meant. Part four: boundaries, limits and skeletons. Boundary and initial values aren't ordinary data points. They define the problem. You can build a candidate that satisfies them exactly: a known part, plus a factor that vanishes on the boundary, times a piece to discover. Then the search looks only for that piece. Limits say even more. If theory says the outflow grows like the square root of the level, write the candidate as c times the square root of h, plus a correction, and let the search work on the correction. A model can fit the measured range beautifully and still grow at the wrong rate. A single error number can't see that. Often you know the architecture of a law, but not all of it. For the tank: area times the rate of change of the level equals inflow minus outflow. Only the outflow law is unknown. So search for the outflow, not for the whole textbook. A grammar can fix the root as a known part plus an unknown part, and leave only the unknown slot open. Then label every piece of the final equation: fixed in advance, constant fitted, structure discovered, or simplified afterwards. Otherwise your assumptions get reported as the machine's discoveries.

transcript.title: When knowledge is wrong
transcript.text: Question. What's more dangerous: a discovery system with no physics, or one with wrong physics, enforced confidently? Pause and decide. The second. A wrong hard rule makes the truth unreachable, and nothing in the score will tell you. Knowledge goes wrong in ordinary ways: the regime changed, the literature model was approximate, a unit was typed wrong, a symmetry is broken, a variable is missing, or a machine suggested something plausible and false. Two diagnostics. First, the weight path: solve again across a range of weights, and watch what changes. We pulled a flexible outflow model toward a prior. With a correct prior, the square root, the error at levels above the data falls from 44 percent to under 2, while the fit inside loosens only a little, from 0.9 to 1.6 cubic centimetres per second. With a wrong prior, outflow proportional to the level, the error above the data stays between 56 and 59 percent, and the fit inside gets about twelve times worse as the weight grows. A conclusion that holds only at one finely tuned weight isn't a conclusion. Second, ablation: run with no prior, with each prior alone, and with all of them. A constraint that changes nothing is clutter. One that improves the fit inside but ruins extrapolation isn't doing what you hoped. And keep a log of where knowledge came from: papers, prompts, retrieved sources, manual edits. A model trained on millions of formulas may hand you a famous law it remembered, rather than one it inferred.

transcript.title: A ladder of knowledge
transcript.text: Part five: the ladder. Forty simulated small tanks, with levels from 20 to 60 centimetres and holes of 4 to 10 millimetres. Then predict ten big tanks: up to two metres of water, and holes up to two centimetres. Rung zero, data only: a flexible quadratic in level, hole size and tank size, with ten constants. It fits the small tanks to about 11 percent. On the big tanks its error is 174 percent, and eight of the ten predicted drain times are negative. Rung one, units: search only over the dimensionless groups. A power law in the two ratios fits the small tanks to 1.6 percent, and predicts the big ones to 1.8 percent. Rung two, signs and trends: drain times must be positive, and grow with the level and with the tank. The power law already obeys them. The quadratic didn't. Rung three, scaling: for small holes, drain time should be proportional to the area ratio. Fix that exponent and fit a single constant: 1.5 percent on the big tanks, and a discharge coefficient of 0.600. Rung four, the skeleton: keep the volume balance, and search only for the outflow law. From level curves, it comes out as the square root of the level, with a coefficient of 0.59. Rung five, the stress test: remove each piece of knowledge in turn. Without units, the prediction collapses. Without the scaling rung, it barely changes: units had already done that work. Every rung is a modeling decision. Compare it with the rung below, and report what each one bought.

transcript.title: Designing the pipeline
transcript.text: So here's how to design a knowledge-aware pipeline. List every piece of knowledge with its source, its confidence, and the range where it holds. Choose a mode for each: hard for necessities, soft or preferential for regularities and hunches. Run the ablations and the weight paths. And keep the provenance of every term. Let's recap. Conservation can be scored, integrated, or built in, and even an unknown invariant can be found from trajectories. Symmetry is cheapest as invariant variables. Shape constraints need a range and a confidence. Boundaries, limits and skeletons let the search focus on what's actually unknown, as long as you label what was supplied. And wrong knowledge, enforced confidently, is the most dangerous kind. In the lab, you'll climb the ladder yourself. Next module: search and optimization, or how to move through an enormous space.

episodes.title: Searching an enormous space
episodes.hook: Sixty throws, one law hidden among hundreds of thousands of formulas, and three searchers with the same budget.
episodes.takeaway: On our first set of throws, genetic programming found the range law in 11 of 20 runs, random search in 3 and enumeration in none. Over 100 runs on five sets of throws it was 28 against 15, and switching crossover off gave 45: rank searchers on many runs, not one.

transcript.title: Sixty throws, three searchers
transcript.text: We throw a ball sixty times, at different speeds and angles, and measure how far it lands. Somewhere among hundreds of thousands of formulas is the range law. Who finds it, with ten thousand tries? Three searchers get the same budget: a blind random searcher, a careful enumerator that tries every formula from small to large, and an evolving population of formulas. By the end of this video you'll know who won, and how much to trust the answer. This is Module four: search and optimization. Part one: the shape of the problem. Part two: searching systematically, with pruning. Part three: genetic programming, the evolutionary workhorse.

transcript.title: Why search is hard
transcript.text: Formally, we want the structure and the constants that minimize the error plus a complexity penalty. Even restricted versions of this problem are known to be computationally hard. So every practical solver bets on some structure: bounded size, good priors, useful building blocks, or learned proposals. And judging a solver by its smallest training error is a trap. A flexible approximation can win on error and still miss the law. Large comparisons show it too: solvers differ in accuracy, in the size of their formulas, and in how often they recover the exact law, and their ranking changes with the benchmark and the metric. Solvers come in families. Enumerators list formulas by complexity. Genetic programming evolves a population. Sequential methods build a formula token by token, guided by a policy or a tree search. Neural generators propose formulas after pretraining. And differentiable methods relax the choice of operators into something continuous. What separates them is the search policy: the rule that decides where the computing effort goes. Which candidates get generated, refined or thrown away, and when to stop.

transcript.title: The shape of the space
transcript.text: Part one: the space. Our language has four binary operations, sine and cosine, and three leaves: the speed v, the angle theta, and the number one. Every candidate also gets a fitted scale and offset, so overall constants come for free. Counted exactly, there are 729,657 trees with at most eight nodes. Most repeat each other: once a scale and offset are allowed, they describe only about 108,000 different candidates, roughly one in seven. The range law, v squared times the sine of twice theta, needs eight nodes: v times v, times the sine of theta plus theta. And this space isn't smooth. One edit can change everything, many edits change nothing, and good formulas sit on narrow ridges between wide plateaus. Picture the neighbours of a formula: change one leaf, swap one operator, replace one branch. From v times v, a single swap gives v plus v, a completely different curve. From v times v times one, removing the one changes nothing at all.

transcript.title: Systematic search and pruning
transcript.text: Part two: systematic search. List candidates in order of complexity, and evaluate each one. Its great virtue is honesty: up to the size you reached, nothing was missed. And it can be pruned. Check syntax, types and units before evaluating. Drop candidates that repeat a function already tried. Bound the size. Screen out variables that don't matter. Guard against division by zero. Order the checks from cheap to expensive: syntax, then units, then a quick numerical check, then fitting constants, then the full data, and only then slow simulation tests. Each stage is a filter with a price. A pruning rule is worth it only when it saves more than it costs, and when the assumption behind it can be defended. Our enumerator skips repeats, so ten thousand evaluations cover every candidate up to six nodes, and part of the seven-node ones. The range law is number 68,655 on its list. So the enumerator is certain to find it, but only after almost seven times the budget. Enumeration can certify that nothing simpler exists. It struggles as soon as the law is a few nodes bigger. Enumeration is most useful inside bigger systems: to search small pieces, to seed a population, or to prove that nothing simpler exists below some size. Pruning has a dark side. A rule that removes the true law turns a belief into an invisible theorem. No amount of optimization brings it back. So record every pruning rule as part of the method, and rerun important discoveries with the rules relaxed.

transcript.title: Genetic programming
transcript.text: Part three: genetic programming. Start with a population of random formulas. Pick parents that fit well. Make children by swapping subtrees between two parents, or by replacing a subtree with a fresh random one. Keep the best, and repeat. The first population is usually grown at several depths, some trees full and some irregular, so that it starts out diverse. Children replace their parents a whole generation at a time, or one by one, and the best can be kept unchanged. Our version: two hundred formulas, ten thousand evaluations, tournaments of four, crossover four times out of five, and the best formula always survives. Every design choice matters: how the first formulas are grown, how parents are chosen, how children are made, who survives, how diversity is kept, and how bloat is controlled. Here's one run. For a while the best error barely moves, near 0.4. Then it slips to 0.3, and after about four thousand four hundred evaluations it drops to 0.045. Later it reaches 0.0225, the noise level. The law itself is now in the population: v times the sine of theta plus theta, times v. Meanwhile the trees grow, from about four nodes on average to about sixteen. And the population's diversity rises, then falls as one family takes over. Look inside good formulas from different runs. The same pieces keep coming back: v times v, and the sine of twice theta, or a sine times a cosine. Genetic programming bets that such pieces can be found apart, and joined by crossover. Pause. Two questions. Does crossover really help here? And does tougher selection, with bigger tournaments, help? Decide before we show you the numbers. We ran every setting a hundred times: five sets of throws, twenty seeds each. Tournaments of two found the law in 33 runs. Tournaments of four, in 28. Tournaments of ten, in 31. Differences that small are within the noise. And crossover? Without it, mutation alone found the law in 45 runs out of 100. With crossover, in 28. In this small language, swapping pieces between formulas did not pay off. We expected the opposite. On our first set of throws, ten seeds without crossover found the law only twice, and crossover looked essential. A hundred runs said otherwise. Small samples tell confident stories. Selection decides which errors count. Tournaments compare total error. Lexicase selection compares parents one data case at a time, in random order, so specialists that are excellent on a few cases survive. Diversity can be measured by the trees, or by what they compute. Semantic methods vary formulas by their behaviour, not just their syntax. And bloat, trees that grow without getting better, is controlled with size limits, with a pressure toward smaller formulas, or by keeping a Pareto front of error against size. Diversity has a structural side too: remove duplicates by hashing, keep niches apart by tree distance, and watch the share of the population that still differs.

transcript.title: Who won
transcript.text: So who won? On our first set of throws, with ten thousand evaluations and twenty seeds each, random search recovered the law in 3 runs, enumeration in none, and genetic programming in 11. Recovered means more than a good fit. The formula must predict throws faster than any in the data, to within two percent. The losers didn't fail quietly. Random search's best formulas fit to about fifteen percent of the spread, and enumeration's best within budget to about twenty four: decent curves, but not the law. Then we drew four more sets of throws: same law, new speeds, new noise. For genetic programming, the worst set gave one success in twenty. The best gave eleven. Over all hundred runs, random search found the law 15 times, and genetic programming 28 times. Enumeration, never. Genetic programming beat blind search here, but by less than one set of throws suggested, and its settings mattered in ways we did not expect. In another language, or with another budget, the ranking can change. That's the subject of the next video.

transcript.title: Recap
transcript.text: Let's recap. Symbolic regression is hard in general, so every solver exploits structure. Enumeration is honest and can certify, but runs out of budget fast. Pruning helps, as long as you record it. Genetic programming adapts, and it beat blind search over a hundred runs. But its success swung with the data, crossover did not pay off here, and its trees bloat. In the lab, you'll race these searchers yourself, on one budget. Next video: other ways to search, and how to compare them fairly.

episodes.title: Other ways to search, and a fair comparison
episodes.hook: Two thirds of the formulas our genetic program evaluated were repeats. A fair comparison starts by counting the waste.
episodes.takeaway: With fitted constants the right structure reaches the noise level (0.0225) and its scale, 0.1023, matches 1/g = 0.1019. Ten seeds made crossover look essential; 100 runs said otherwise. Compare searchers on equal terms, over many seeds and data sets.

transcript.title: Two thirds were repeats
transcript.text: Two thirds of the formulas our genetic programming evaluated had already been evaluated before. Search is full of waste, and fairness starts with counting it. In this video: building formulas one token at a time, learned and differentiable search, constants inside the loop, keeping several answers, speed-ups, when to stop, and how to compare searchers fairly. Last video, genetic programming beat blind search, by a margin that swung with the data. This video asks what else is possible, and how to make a race fair.

transcript.title: Sequential and tree search
transcript.text: Part one: sequential search. Instead of whole trees, build a formula one token at a time, in prefix order. Each partial formula is a state, and each next token is an action. A policy, often a neural network, gives probabilities to the next tokens. Reinforcement learning rewards it for good finished formulas, and risk-seeking variants learn only from the best few percent, because we want the best formula, not a good average. Monte Carlo tree search treats the same choices as a game tree. It balances exploiting branches that already look promising against exploring branches it hardly knows. And partial formulas can be checked early. A branch that already breaks the units, or can't close within the length limit, is pruned before it's finished. The hard part is credit assignment: a token chosen early only gets its reward when the whole formula is finished and fitted.

transcript.title: Learned and differentiable search
transcript.text: Part two: learned and differentiable search. A transformer pretrained on millions of synthetic formulas can propose candidates for new data in a fraction of a second. But that speed was paid for in advance, during pretraining, and its proposals lean toward the kinds of formulas it was trained on. Report both costs, and ask how far your data are from its training. Differentiable methods relax the discrete choice. Each node becomes a soft mixture of operators, with weights trained by gradient descent, then sharpened until one operator wins. The catch is the final rounding: the best soft mixture can be far from the best single formula. Always refit after discretizing. Many systems mix these ideas: a network proposes formulas, an evolutionary search refines them, and the network learns again from the refined results. Training data matter: if most training formulas were polynomials, a generator will keep proposing polynomials, even for a pendulum.

transcript.title: Constants inside the loop
transcript.text: Part three: constants. Structure and constants are coupled. A correct structure with bad constants looks wrong, and gets thrown away. Take the right structure for our throws, with random constants: its typical error is more than ten times the spread of the data. With fitted constants: 0.0225, the noise level. A wrong structure, v squared times theta, fitted just as carefully, still scores 0.67. And the fitted scale comes out as 0.1023. One over g is 0.1019. The fitted constant carries physics. So every candidate deserves a fair shot at its constants: linear least squares when they enter linearly, a few local steps otherwise, and restarts when the landscape is rough. Constant fitting has a price too. In many systems it takes most of the compute, so it belongs in the accounting when methods are compared.

transcript.title: Several answers: the Pareto front
transcript.text: Part four: keep several answers. Here's the final population of one run, as error against size. Its Pareto front has four members: v alone, v squared, the range law with eight nodes, and a nineteen-node formula that's better by a hair. The knee is obvious. From eight nodes to nineteen, the error drops by just two ten-thousandths, to 0.0223. That's noise, not physics. Choose from the front with held-out data and the checks from Module one, not with the training error. Some methods search the front directly, keeping error and complexity as separate objectives, sometimes with more: a physics residual, a smoothness score, or the error on held-out data.

transcript.title: Speed, stopping and reporting
transcript.text: Part five: speed. Most of the cost is evaluation, so the tricks are about evaluating less. Cache results: two thirds of our candidates were repeats. Take a quick look first: a check on ten of the sixty points would have flagged 37 percent of candidates as hopeless before the full evaluation. Vectorize, compile, and run in parallel, but remember that the slowest serial part limits any speed-up. Even the timing of evaluations matters. Asynchronous workers don't wait for a whole generation to finish, and that changes the evolution itself, not just the speed. Simplify before you evaluate: when two candidates reduce to the same canonical form, one evaluation serves both. Part six: when to stop, and what to report. Stop on a budget, on a front that has stopped improving, or on a target error. And state which one in advance. Report the language, the budget in evaluations and in time, the number of seeds, the constant fitting, the simplification rules, the full Pareto fronts, and the success rate across seeds, not just the best run. Watch diagnostics while it runs: the front over time, the population's diversity, the share of duplicates, and how often constant fitting fails. They tell you whether a search is stuck, or just slow. And seeds belong in the report: with the same seed and the same software, anyone should get exactly your front. One lucky seed is an anecdote. Many seeds, on several sets of data, are evidence. Pause. One searcher returns its answers in a second, another takes an hour. Is the first one cheaper? Think about what might be hidden. Not necessarily. The fast one may have spent weeks pretraining. A fair comparison counts offline and online cost separately, and reports both. Hardware counts too: a run on many processors and a run on one are different budgets, even with the same number of evaluations. Memory and engineering count as well. A method that needs a cache of millions of formulas, or a specialised compiler, carries costs that a count of evaluations never shows.

transcript.title: A fair comparison
transcript.text: Part seven: a fair comparison. Give every searcher identical data, language, constant fitting, budget, and number of seeds. Then measure several things: how often each recovers the true structure, not just a good fit; error on held-out and extrapolated data; complexity; time to the first success; and how much effort went to repeats. Then remove pieces, and use enough runs. On one set of throws and ten seeds, removing crossover looked like a disaster: two successes. Over a hundred runs, it was the best setting we tried: 45 successes. With crossover, 28. A claim that one method is better is incomplete until it says: better at what, on which problems, and with which budget. Run a version without constant fitting, and one without removing duplicates. The differences show how much of the success came from the search itself, and how much from the machinery around it. Summarize with several views, not one winning number: error against time, the final fronts, and recovery rates across seeds. And state the scope. Our arena had two variables, one law and sixty throws. A real study needs several problems, noise levels and held-out regions before a ranking means much. Our own runs show why. With identical settings, standard genetic programming succeeded in only one seed out of twenty on one set of throws. On another set, it succeeded in eleven.

transcript.title: Recap
transcript.text: Let's recap. Sequential and tree-search methods build formulas token by token. Learned generators are fast, but carry their training with them. Differentiable search must be rounded, and refit. Constants need a fair fit inside the loop. Several answers should be kept on a Pareto front. And speed comes from evaluating less: caching, quick checks, parallel work. And compare searchers on equal terms, across many seeds. In the lab, you'll do exactly that. Next module: scientific data, noise, and experimental design.

episodes.title: Is the data ready?
episodes.hook: One phone video of a weight on a spring, three careful pipelines, three different laws. The difference is everything before the search.
episodes.takeaway: With 1 mm of tracking noise at 30 frames per second, finite differences gave accelerations with about 2 m/s² of noise against a real signal below 0.8, and lost the damping; filming at 120 frames per second made it about 17 times worse. Smoothing found the right terms with damping 13% too small; the weak form found −16.1·x − 0.40·v.

transcript.title: One video, three laws
transcript.text: We film a weight bouncing on a spring with a phone, at thirty frames per second. The tracking is good to about a millimetre. From that one video, three careful pipelines return three different laws. Finite differences say: a equals minus 17.8 x. The damping has vanished. Smoothing says: minus 15 x, minus 0.35 v. A weak form says: minus 16.1 x, minus 0.40 v. The law we simulated is minus 16 x, minus 0.4 v. Same data, same search. The difference is everything that happened before the search. This video is about that part. This is Module five: scientific data, noise, and experimental design. Part one: is the data adequate? Part two: noise and sampling. Part three: derivatives, and how to avoid them.

transcript.title: Is the data adequate?
transcript.text: A camera never returns the state of a system. It returns a measurement of it: a function of the state, the settings and the calibration, plus error. So every discovery depends on three things: the law, the experiment, and the measurement. Ask six questions before any search. Quantity: enough independent observations? Coverage: do they reach the states where candidate laws differ? Resolution: are the fast scales resolved? Signal to noise. Observability: are the needed variables measured at all? And excitation: was the system pushed hard enough? More data is not a universal remedy. Measuring somewhere new often beats measuring the same place again. Here's an example. Suppose our spring stiffens when it is stretched far: an extra term, minus four hundred x cubed. At a two centimetre swing, that term is about one percent of the force. At eight centimetres, it is sixteen percent. We estimated the cubic coefficient from small swings, two hundred times, with fresh noise each time. The estimates scattered widely. Some were negative. Some were three times the truth. From eight centimetre swings, every estimate landed within five percent of four hundred. No optimizer can create information the experiment never collected. The problem here isn't noise. It's support. Two more questions are about the experiment itself. Observability: if the mechanism needs a variable you never measured, the search will invent complicated stand-ins built from the variables you did measure. And excitation: a coefficient on something that barely changes is barely identified. Different starts, forcings or amplitudes are what separate one candidate term from another.

transcript.title: Noise and sampling
transcript.text: Part two: noise. The textbook picture is independent noise added to the response. Real data are messier. Error in the inputs, not just the outputs. Noise that grows with the signal. Errors that are correlated in time. An instrument that slowly drifts. Values clipped at a sensor's limit. And gaps that are not random. Each one does its own damage. Input error biases coefficients. Correlated errors make a sample look bigger than it is. Drift invents terms that depend on time. Clipping creates fake plateaus. And measurement noise is not the same as a random system. If the system itself is random, that randomness is part of the law you are looking for. Report noise against a scale. Five percent of what? For our camera: about one millimetre on a five centimetre swing, so two percent of the amplitude. Sampling decides which scales you can see at all. Our spring swings with a period of about 1.6 seconds. Sample it about every 1.4 seconds, and the points trace a slow wave with a period of almost 16 seconds. That's aliasing. The samples look smooth, convincing, and completely wrong. A search would happily fit a law for a slow oscillator that doesn't exist. Gaps have geometry too. Losing a random fifth of the frames thins the data. Losing the end of the recording removes the slow decay, exactly where damping shows itself. And dense is not the same as independent. A camera at a thousand frames per second does not give a thousand independent observations per second of a slow swing.

transcript.title: Derivatives amplify noise
transcript.text: Part three: derivatives. The camera gives positions. The law is about acceleration. Somewhere, positions must become velocities and accelerations. The simplest way is finite differences: the change between neighbouring frames, divided by the time step. For acceleration, a second difference, divided by the time step squared. And that's where noise explodes. With one millimetre of tracking noise at thirty frames per second, the noise in the computed acceleration is about two metres per second squared. The real acceleration never exceeds 0.8. Pause. Should we film in slow motion, at a hundred and twenty frames per second, to get better accelerations? Decide before we show you. It gets worse, about seventeen times worse: from about two, to about thirty four. Dividing by a smaller time step squared amplifies the same millimetre more. Finer sampling shrinks the approximation error, and multiplies the noise.

transcript.title: Smoothing and weak forms
transcript.text: The usual fix is smoothing: fit a smooth curve through the noisy positions, then differentiate the curve. Here, a local cubic fitted over half a second of frames. The acceleration noise drops from about two to about four hundredths. And the search now finds the right two terms. But look at the numbers: minus 15 x, and minus 0.35 v. Both are too small. Smoothing is a modelling choice. It decides what counts as signal. A wider window removes more noise, and more of the oscillation. With a quarter second window, the damping was off by four percent. With a second and a half, by sixty two percent. Or avoid differentiating the data at all. Multiply the law by a smooth bump that is zero at both ends of a window, and integrate. Integration by parts moves the derivatives from the noisy data onto the bump, which we know exactly. Acceleration times the bump becomes position times the bump's second derivative. No noisy derivative is ever computed. On the same video, the weak form gives minus 16.1 x, minus 0.40 v. Over forty noise draws, its damping stayed within about one percent, up to two millimetres of noise. But the window is a choice too. Narrow windows keep detail and average little noise. Wide windows average more, and can blur different regimes together. The window is part of the scientific design.

transcript.title: A sweep, and many recordings
transcript.text: Here's the whole sweep, with forty noise draws at each level. Finite differences recover the right two terms up to a quarter of a millimetre of noise, and never from half a millimetre on. Smoothing and the weak form keep the right terms much longer. At eight millimetres, smoothing still found them in nineteen draws of forty, and the weak form in all forty. But up to four millimetres, smoothing's damping stays about thirteen percent too small, because that error comes from the window, not from the noise. Right terms with wrong numbers, or good numbers with an extra term: structure and coefficients are separate questions. Report both. One recording rarely explores a whole system. Several starts, amplitudes or forcings cover more of the states where candidate laws differ. But keep the grouping. Frames from one recording are close cousins. When you test, split recordings, not rows. And before pooling experiments, ask whether the same law should hold in all of them. Pool different regimes, and you get an average law that fits none of them.

transcript.title: Recap
transcript.text: Let's recap. Adequacy depends on the claim: quantity, coverage, resolution, signal to noise, observability, and excitation. Small swings could not see the stiffening term at all. Noise comes in many shapes, so report it against a scale. Sampling can alias a fast swing into a slow one. And derivatives amplify noise: smoothing trades noise for bias, and weak forms move the derivative onto a function we know. In the lab, you'll damage our spring's data yourself. Next video: making better data, from synthetic enrichment to experiments chosen on purpose.

episodes.title: Making better data
episodes.hook: A model filled in a swing nobody measured, and the stiffening term flipped sign. One real recording fixed it.
episodes.takeaway: Over 40 noise draws, a model-generated 8 cm swing turned the stiffening coefficient (truth 400) into about −59 every time, while one real 8 cm recording gave about 402. Random-row and whole-recording splits could not tell a flexible polynomial from the law's form (7% vs 7%); an amplitude split could (58% vs 7%).

transcript.title: A swing nobody measured
transcript.text: Our spring stiffens at large swings, but we only measured swings up to four centimetres. So we let a model fill in an eight centimetre swing, and gave the search real and synthetic data together. Over forty noise draws, the search reported a stiffening coefficient near minus 59, every time. The true value is 400. With one real recording at eight centimetres instead, it found about 402. The synthetic swing looked smooth and physical. It carried the assumptions of the model that made it, and nothing new about the spring. In this video. Part one: what synthetic data can and cannot do. Part two: choosing the next experiment. Part three: validation splits that match the claim. Part four: a data-readiness protocol.

transcript.title: What synthetic data can and cannot do
transcript.text: Separate two things: choosing where to measure, and producing the value there. If a method picks a new swing and you then run that experiment, you have new evidence. If a model supplies the value as well, the point is synthetic. Synthetic data can still help. It can fill sparse regions, stabilize derivatives, or test a search under conditions you control. But every synthetic point is a descendant of a model. Enrichment can add numerical resolution without adding any structural information. Ten thousand generated points can reinforce a distortion more strongly than a hundred careful measurements. Even inside the measured range, support can be thin. Measurements bunched around two settings leave a gap between them. A generated point in that gap is inside the range, and still far from any real observation. Synthetic points also flatter the error bars. Each one counts like a measurement, so the fit looks more certain, while no new information has arrived. Generators differ in what they assume: small perturbations or interpolation, a statistical copy of the data, a model of outputs given inputs, a mechanistic simulator, or a learned generator with physics built in. Each one brings a prior. If a reconstruction enforces energy conservation, finding a law that conserves energy afterwards is not a discovery. It was built in upstream. And a law fitted only to simulator output is a law of the simulator. That can be very useful, as a compact surrogate. But testing it against nature needs measurements the simulator never saw. Pretrained generators carry a prior too: millions of training formulas decide which shapes feel familiar. Report the training distribution, so readers can tell prior exposure from evidence. The strongest use of synthetic data is the honest one: a controlled test, where the truth is known and the difficulty is turned up on purpose. Every number in this module came from exactly that kind of test. So every use of synthetic data needs a control: rerun without it, keep a flag on every generated point, and report the share of synthetic to real. For our spring, that control catches the problem at once. Real data alone gave about 400, with a wide spread. The synthetic swing flipped the sign, in all forty draws. The spread tells the same story. Across the draws, real data alone scattered widely around 400. With the one new recording added, the scatter shrank more than six times.

transcript.title: Choosing the next experiment
transcript.text: Part two: choose the next experiment on purpose. Fit the competing candidate laws, then ask where they disagree the most. From our small swings we have two candidates: a plain spring, and a stiffening one. Up to about three centimetres, they predict almost the same force. Beyond that, they pull apart faster and faster. So we run one swing at the largest amplitude we can safely reach. One recording settles a question that more small swings never could. The rule depends on the goal. Uncertainty for prediction. Disagreement between candidate laws for choosing a mechanism. Novelty for coverage. And you can choose more than x: starts, forcing, sensor positions, sampling times. Record the rule that chose each experiment. Otherwise nobody can tell whether the law was robust, or steered into the data. And when the procedure itself steers where to measure, the record has to say so, or a reader may credit the law with a robustness that was really the design. And notice the cost. More small swings would add more frames, but every one of them would sit where the two candidates already agree.

transcript.title: Splits that match the claim
transcript.text: Pause. A flexible model and the true law's form both score about seven percent error on frames held out at random. Which one would you trust at a bigger swing? Hold out a random fifth of the frames: 7.0 and 6.8 percent. Hold out a whole recording: 6.6 and 6.1 percent. Neither test tells them apart. Now train on swings up to four centimetres, and test on eight. The law's form: seven percent. The flexible polynomial: fifty eight percent. These are medians over forty noise draws. The split decides which question you answered. Random rows test interpolation. Whole recordings test new starts. Held-out amplitudes test extrapolation. Match the split to the claim. And keep preprocessing on the training side. Smoothing windows, normalization and synthetic points must never be tuned on the test data. Validation has three layers. Predictive: does the law forecast measurements? Structural: when the truth is known, are the right terms recovered? Scientific: does the law survive tests that played no part in finding it? These layers can disagree. A wrong expression can predict well over a narrow range, while a plausible one can lose a little accuracy inside the data, and extrapolate far better. Our spring shows all three. On random frames, the flexible polynomial predicted as well as the law. Its terms were not the spring's terms, so it failed the structural test. And at the bigger swing, it failed the scientific one.

transcript.title: A data-readiness protocol
transcript.text: Part four: a data-readiness protocol. Its job is simple: fix the data decisions before the search, so they cannot drift toward a favourite equation. Start with the claim, stated precisely. For example: one law for this spring, for swings up to eight centimetres, that predicts recordings from new starts. Then the measurement chain: what was measured, and what was derived. An acceleration computed twice from video is not a measurement with the same uncertainty as position. Then the rest: support, uncertainty from repeated measurements rather than from residuals, at least two derivative pipelines, splits fixed in advance, and a flag on every value: measured, derived, interpolated, or simulated. If the law changes whenever one reasonable preprocessing choice changes, the honest conclusion is that the data do not yet identify a stable law. The protocol is not a cage. If the first search reveals a missing variable or an unstable derivative, revise the protocol in the open, and start a new analysis. Never replace the old one silently. Here's our spring through the protocol. The claim: one law for swings up to eight centimetres. Measured: position only, with about a millimetre of noise. Derived: velocity and acceleration, three ways. Finite differences lost the damping. Smoothing found the right terms with numbers that were too small. The weak form found both. When pipelines agree on structure but not on numbers, that is itself a finding to report. Splits by recording and by amplitude, fixed in advance. No synthetic points in the final fit, and the enriched run reported as a warning. So what we would report is narrow, and honest: a stiffening spring, with a coefficient near 400 once the large swing was measured, valid for swings up to eight centimetres, from new starts.

transcript.title: Recap
transcript.text: Let's recap. Synthetic data adds computation, not evidence: control it, flag it, and report its share. Pretraining is a prior. Choose new experiments where candidate laws disagree: one well-placed recording beat many repeats. Splits must match the claim. And lock the data decisions before the search. In the lab, you'll choose the next swing yourself. Next module: static laws and interpretable surrogates.

episodes.title: Scaling laws, correlations and closures
episodes.hook: Nine pendulums on three worlds fall on one curve before any search begins.
episodes.takeaway: Units turned five quantities into two numbers, and nine pendulums collapsed to within 0.46%. A guessed power law gave a meaningless exponent (2.33); a search found two mechanisms, v and v³, with physical coefficients. Two closures that fit equally well stopped a coasting bike 15 s apart.

transcript.title: Nine pendulums, one curve
transcript.text: We timed pendulums on three worlds, Earth, Mars and the Moon, with three lengths each, at swings from small to very large. The periods spread over a factor of eight. Now plot the period times the square root of g over L, against the swing angle. All nine pendulums fall on one curve. Two lines of algebra did that, before any search began. This module is about static laws: one formula from inputs to an output, with no time derivative. Some are laws, some are correlations, some stand in for a simulator. Knowing which is half the job. This is Module six: static laws and interpretable surrogates. Part one: dimensionless structure. Part two: correlations, searched instead of guessed. Part three: closures that live inside a simulation. Part four: descriptors.

transcript.title: Three kinds of static formula
transcript.text: Three kinds of static formula look alike on paper. A candidate law claims to be part of the mechanism. An empirical correlation summarizes behaviour over a stated range. A surrogate approximates another computer model. The same equation can move between these labels only when new evidence changes the claim. And the label decides the search: units may be non-negotiable for a law, while a surrogate can afford an extra term if it is fast and smooth.

transcript.title: Dimensionless structure
transcript.text: Part one: dimensionless structure. A pendulum's period could depend on its length, gravity, its mass, and the swing angle. Only length, time and mass are involved, and nothing else carries mass, so mass drops out. So the law must read: the period times the square root of g over L equals some function of the angle alone. Five quantities became two numbers, before a single timing. The general rule is the Buckingham pi theorem. Count the quantities, subtract the number of independent units, and you get the number of dimensionless groups. Here: five quantities, three units, two groups. Engineers lean on the same idea every day. Groups like the Reynolds number let one correlation cover pipes of every size, and fluids of every kind. Now the search looks for one function of one variable, and its constants can't quietly depend on whether you measured in metres or in feet. In our data, a small swing takes about 1.1 seconds for a short pendulum on Earth, and about 5.4 seconds for a long one on the Moon. In the new coordinates, the nine pendulums lie on one curve, rising from two pi at small swings. The collapse is also a test. If the points had refused to collapse, something missing from our list, like friction or a heavy string, would be shaping the period. Ours did collapse. The points scatter around one curve by about half a percent, the size of our timing noise. Nothing else is left to explain. But dimensional analysis doesn't pick a unique set of groups. Many valid combinations exist, and some make the remaining search far easier than others. And a perfect collapse is not a mechanism. It shows that the runs share one representation. Why that representation works needs other evidence.

transcript.title: Correlations: guessed or searched
transcript.text: Part two: engineering correlations. A cyclist's power at a steady speed on flat ground. We simulated a hundred rides, most of them fast, with four percent noise. The classic move is to guess a template, power equals C times speed to the power b, and fit C and b. Templates like this are everywhere in engineering, and within a narrow range they can fit well. Here, the best fit gives b equal to 2.33. That exponent means nothing physical. It is a compromise between two mechanisms, and it misses both regimes: by about eight percent at low speed, and six and a half at high speed. Fit only the slow rides, and b drops to 1.8. Fit only the fast ones, and it rises to 2.6. The exponent records which rides you happened to collect. Now search instead: a small library of powers of speed, and thresholded least squares. The search keeps exactly two terms: speed, and speed cubed. Their coefficients are physical. The first gives a rolling coefficient of 0.0051. The second gives a drag area of 0.346 square metres. We simulated 0.005 and 0.35. Search found the structure the template had assumed away: two mechanisms, added. The errors fell to five percent at low speed, and three at high speed. And the search shows its Pareto front. One term, speed cubed, leaves a median error of 9.2 percent. Two terms: 3.2 percent. A third or a fourth term buys only a tenth of a percent. The bend is at two. Build correlations around regimes: weigh slow and fast rides by how the formula will be used, not by how many of each you happened to record. And choose from the front, near its bend.

transcript.title: Closures inside a simulation
transcript.text: Part three: closures. A closure is a formula that lives inside a larger simulation: a stress law, a friction law, a turbulence correction. It must be judged as a regression, and as a component. Back to our cyclist. We fitted the resistance force two ways, on rides between four and fourteen metres per second: the true form, a constant plus a speed squared term, and a cubic polynomial. Both fit the rides equally well. Pause. Put each closure into a simulation of a bike coasting from six metres per second with no pedalling. Will they agree on when it stops? They don't. With the fitted true form, the bike stops after about 83 seconds, close to the 85 of the law we simulated. With the polynomial, after about 98. The polynomial invented a lower resistance at slow speeds it never saw: near zero speed, 2.7 newtons instead of 4.2. Offline accuracy is not closure validity. A limit check would have caught it before any simulation. At zero speed, only rolling resistance is left: the mass, times g, times the rolling coefficient. That is 4.2 newtons, not 2.7. And the simulation went exactly where the data wasn't. After about twenty seconds, the coasting bike is below four metres per second, and it stays there for the rest of the run. Testing a closure on stored data is called a priori testing. Running it inside the solver is a posteriori testing. You need both, and they often disagree. Closures carry constraints too. A correction that must keep a sign can be written as a factor, the exponential of a learned term. And candidates that break physical rules can be filtered before any expensive run.

transcript.title: Descriptors
transcript.text: Part four: descriptors. In materials science the goal is often not a universal law, but a compact combination of properties that organizes a huge space of candidates. A searched descriptor, built from quantities like atomic radii, elastic moduli or energies, can rank materials for screening, and hint at what matters. That is worth a lot. A good descriptor can shrink a long list of candidate materials to a short one worth making in the lab, even before anyone knows why it works. Methods such as SISSO build millions of candidate combinations from basic properties, screen them, and keep a handful with sparse regression. With that many candidates, some will fit by chance. So test on whole families of materials the search never saw. And read a descriptor as a hypothesis about useful coordinates, not as a mechanism, until independent evidence says why it works.

transcript.title: Recap
transcript.text: Let's recap. Decide first whether you want a law, a correlation, or a surrogate. Dimensionless groups shrink the search: for our pendulum, five quantities became two numbers. Searching beat guessing a template: two mechanisms, added, with physical coefficients, chosen at the bend of the front. And closures must pass their limit checks, and be tested inside the simulation they will live in. In the lab, you'll collapse the pendulums yourself. Next video: residuals, surrogates, and the limits of a formula.

episodes.title: Residuals, surrogates and the limits of a formula
episodes.hook: The textbook pendulum formula is within 1% up to 1.8 rad, and 20% off at 2.9.
episodes.takeaway: A residual search next to the small-swing law found 0.0604·θ², against the known 1/16 = 0.0625. The series ran more than a million times faster than our integrator and held within 1% up to 1.8 rad; the cheap law plus three expensive runs gave 1.7% worst error, against 3.6% from the runs alone. State every formula's envelope, then attack it.

transcript.title: Where formulas stop working
transcript.text: The textbook correction for a pendulum's period matches the exact value within one percent, for swings up to 1.8 radians. At 2.9 radians it predicts 1.78 times the small-swing period. The truth is 2.24. Black boxes trained on swings up to two radians do no better. A nearest-neighbour model predicts 1.25 for every larger swing. A degree eight polynomial predicts 7.3 at 2.8 radians. Every formula has a validity envelope. This video is about finding it, and about formulas that live next to a theory, or stand in for a simulator. In this video. Part one: residuals, learning what a theory misses. Part two: symbolic surrogates. Part three: combining cheap and expensive models. Part four: envelopes, stress tests and black boxes.

transcript.title: Residuals: learning what a theory misses
transcript.text: Part one: residuals. When a trusted theory exists, don't throw it away. Learn only what it misses: the measured value minus the theory, or their ratio. For the pendulum, the small-swing law is the theory. We divided each measured period by it, and searched for that ratio as a function of the angle, using swings up to one and a half radians. The theory carries the units and the big picture, so the search only has to find a small, dimensionless number close to one. That is a far easier target than the whole law. We offered only even powers of the angle. A swing to the left takes as long as a swing to the right, so the correction must be symmetric. Symmetry shrank the library before the search began. Here is what the search returned. One, plus 0.0604 times theta squared, plus 0.0049 times theta to the fourth. The known series starts with one, plus one sixteenth theta squared. And one sixteenth is 0.0625. How sure are these numbers? We resampled the data four hundred times. The squared term stayed between 0.056 and 0.064, and one sixteenth sits inside that range. The fourth-power term is far less sure. It ranged from 0.003 to 0.007, and the series value of 0.0036 sits near the lower edge. It soaks up higher terms that the data cannot separate. When we offered theta to the sixth, its coefficient came out at essentially zero. The correction has an immediate meaning: how much a big swing slows the pendulum down. That's the appeal of residual laws: the theory stays, and the new term is small and readable. Choose the form by the suspected error: an added term for a missing process, a ratio or a log ratio for a missing factor. And remember that residuals also hold noise and bias, not only new physics.

transcript.title: Symbolic surrogates
transcript.text: Part two: symbolic surrogates. Our expensive simulator integrates the pendulum's equation numerically: about 5,600 small steps for each period. The series gives a period in a single line. In our Python code it was more than a million times faster: tens of milliseconds for the integrator, tens of nanoseconds for the formula. And it matched the integrator within one percent, up to 1.8 radians. Our own fitted correction, from noisy data, held within one percent up to 2.1 radians, further than the textbook terms, because its larger fourth-power term stands in for the missing ones. Further, but still finite. A surrogate is judged by its purpose: speed and accuracy, for the quantity a downstream calculation needs, over a declared domain. Not by whether it is the law. Surrogates pay off in repeated work: calibration, uncertainty propagation, design, control. A formula is also differentiable, and easy to embed anywhere. Where should the expensive runs go when you build one? We used an even grid. Spending runs where the formula's error is largest is cheaper: the active learning of Module five, aimed at a simulator.

transcript.title: Cheap and expensive models
transcript.text: Part three: multi-fidelity. Cheap models are plentiful but biased. Expensive ones are accurate but rare. Combine them. Here the cheap model is the small-swing law, free everywhere. The expensive one is the integrator, run only three times. We learned a correction to the cheap model from those three runs. Across swings up to 2.3 radians, the combined model's worst error was 1.7 percent. A quadratic through the three expensive runs alone: 3.6 percent. And the correction it learned from three runs was 0.061 times theta squared. Again, that is close to one sixteenth. Why did it work? The cheap law is exactly right at small swings, so the correction must vanish there. Building that in left only two numbers to learn from three runs. The quadratic had to learn everything from the same three. The cheap model supplies the shape, and the expensive runs supply the correction. But a biased cheap model can also mislead, so check the combination on expensive runs it never saw.

transcript.title: Black boxes beyond the data
transcript.text: Pause. The nearest-neighbour model, the polynomial, and a fitted series all match the training swings well. Which one would you trust at 2.5 radians? None of them, fully. At 2.5 radians the truth is 1.64. The fitted series says 1.57. The nearest-neighbour model says 1.25. The polynomial says 2.54. Just past the training edge, at 2.2 radians, the series is off by under two percent, the polynomial by under four, and the nearest-neighbour model by twelve. The black boxes fail silently: one flattens, one explodes. The series fails gradually, and its form tells you why: a polynomial in the angle cannot follow a period that grows without limit as the swing approaches the top. Near the top, the period really does grow without limit. A formula fitted below two radians cannot know that. Declare the envelope.

transcript.title: Validity envelopes and stress tests
transcript.text: Part four: validity envelopes. State where a formula holds: the range of each input, the combinations covered, and the tolerance. Our series holds within one percent up to 1.8 radians. Its first term alone, only to about 1.3. And the envelope depends on the tolerance you declare. At one part in a thousand, the series holds only to about 1.3 radians. At five percent, it holds to about 2.4. Then stress-test it. Push the inputs toward the edges, check the limits, check symmetries, and test points inside the range but far from any data. Our series passes the limit test: at zero swing, the ratio is one. It passes the symmetry test by construction. It fails the edge test: near the top, it stays finite. So the report reads: the period ratio is one, plus theta squared over sixteen, plus eleven theta to the fourth over three thousand and seventy two. Valid within one percent for swings up to 1.8 radians. Checked against a numerical integrator. A formula used outside its envelope isn't a law being tested. It's a guess with good handwriting. Black boxes are often more accurate inside the data. Compare them fairly: the same splits, the same inputs, the same extrapolation tests, and accuracy reported against complexity. Prefer the symbolic model when its behaviour must be checked, embedded, or extrapolated, or when its terms answer a scientific question. Prefer the black box when only accuracy inside the data matters. Black boxes have envelopes too. They just don't print them. Report where the training data lie, and treat every prediction outside them as a guess. And they can work together: a black box can teach a formula. That is a topic for Module ten.

transcript.title: Recap
transcript.text: Let's recap. Residual laws keep the theory and learn what it misses. Here, a correction close to one sixteenth of the angle squared. Symbolic surrogates trade a little accuracy for enormous speed, over a declared domain. Multi-fidelity combines a cheap model's shape with an expensive model's correction. Black boxes and formulas deserve the same tests: the same splits, the same edges, and an honest envelope for each. Every formula has an envelope: find it, state it, and stress-test it. In the lab, you'll draw ours. Next module: ordinary differential equations.

episodes.title: Finding the right-hand side
episodes.hook: A beaker that keeps time: plain least squares writes twenty terms for its law, and fits a little better than the truth. The law has five.
episodes.takeaway: At 1% noise the weak form found the clock's five terms in 39 of 40 noise draws, finite differences in 22, smoothing in none. Thresholds from 0.2 to 1.2 all worked; one settled run on the cycle never found the law, six starting mixtures found it 39 times in 40, and with the feed in the library it was found in all 40.

transcript.title: A chemical clock
transcript.text: A beaker that keeps time. Feed it two chemicals at a steady rate, and its colour swings back and forth, about once every six and a half minutes. Chemists call reactions like this chemical clocks. We simulated one with a textbook model called the Brusselator, measured two concentrations every three seconds, and added one percent noise. Then we asked a computer for the law. Plain least squares wrote twenty terms, and fit our data a little better than the truth did. The real law has five terms. This video is about finding those five: the right-hand side of a differential equation. This is Module seven: ordinary differential equations. Part one: derivatives are inferred objects. Part two: sparse libraries and a threshold. Part three: three ways to pose the fit. Part four: many runs and many regimes.

transcript.title: Derivatives are inferred objects
transcript.text: An ordinary differential equation says how fast each quantity changes, given the current state. In our clock, the rate of change of X depends on X and Y, and so does the rate of change of Y. That rule, the right-hand side, is what we want. But no instrument measures a rate of change. We measure concentrations. Every derivative in a discovery pipeline is estimated, and the estimate has its own errors and its own assumptions. Finite differences assume that samples are close enough for a straight line between them. In our sixth run, X starts out changing at fifty-one units per minute. With a sample every three seconds, the difference quotient misses by up to about five, with no noise at all. Smoothing assumes that the curve is gentle inside its window. Our window was half a minute, longer than that fast start. With perfect data, smoothing first and differentiating second already breaks the search. The weak form avoids the derivative. Multiply the equation by a smooth bump, integrate, and move the derivative onto the bump by integration by parts. What's left needs only the measured concentrations. Across forty noise draws at one percent noise, the weak form found the right terms thirty-nine times. Finite differences found them twenty-two times. Smoothing, never. A derivative is a measurement you didn't make. Treat it like one, with error bars and a stated method.

transcript.title: Sparse libraries and a threshold
transcript.text: Part two: sparse libraries. We don't know the right-hand side, so we list candidate pieces: a constant, X, Y, and every product up to degree three. That's ten terms for each equation. Then we write each rate as a weighted sum of those pieces and fit the weights. That's a linear problem, fast and exact. But ordinary least squares keeps every term, and that's how we got twenty. Most laws in physics and chemistry use only a few of the possible pieces. So we look for a sparse answer: fit, drop every term whose weight falls below a threshold, refit with what's left, and repeat until nothing changes. On our clock data, that loop returns this. dX by dt equals one, minus 3.5 times X, plus X squared Y. And dY by dt equals 2.5 times X, minus X squared Y. That's the law we simulated, to two decimals. Each term reads as chemistry. The one is the steady feed. Minus 3.5 X is X being used up: 2.5 parts turn into Y, one part leaves. And X squared Y is the step where two X and one Y make a third X. That feedback makes the clock tick. The threshold is the knob that matters. We tried nine values, each on forty noise draws. Set it too low and nothing is dropped. Eighteen or nineteen terms survive, and the law is never found. Set it too high and a real term goes too. Four terms, never right. In between, a wide window, from 0.2 to 1.2, finds the law in thirty-seven to forty draws out of forty. A window that wide is good news. A result that appears at one magic threshold only is a warning. And notice what the threshold didn't do: improve the fit. The twenty-term formula fit our data slightly better than the truth. Fit alone can't choose here. Sparsity, chemistry and later tests must.

transcript.title: Three ways to pose the fit
transcript.text: Part three: three ways to pose the fit. Derivative matching estimates the rates and regresses them on the library. The weak form matches integrals against test functions. Trajectory matching simulates the candidate equations and compares whole curves with the data. We kept the five true terms fixed and compared the three on the numbers alone, ten noise draws each. At one percent noise, the worst coefficient error was 5.4 percent for finite differences. The weak form got it down to 0.6 percent. And trajectory matching got it to 0.08 percent. At five times the noise: 14 percent, 4.7 percent, and 0.3 percent. Matching whole trajectories weighs every sample against the noise, and never differentiates anything. So why not always simulate? Because it's slow, and because the error surface has more than one valley. Every guess needs a full simulation, and an oscillation that's slightly off in timing can score worse than one that's far off. Here's a real slice. Take a one-hour recording, and vary only the feedback coefficient, whose true value is one. The error has five valleys. A local search that starts outside 0.87 to 1.12 settles in a wrong one. Started from the weak-form estimate, it went straight to the law. A practical recipe: let a fast, robust formulation choose the terms and a starting point, then let trajectory matching polish the numbers.

transcript.title: Many runs, many regimes
transcript.text: Part four: many runs and many regimes. Pause here. Which data would you rather have: one long recording of the clock, ticking steadily, or six short runs from six different starting mixtures? Once the clock settles onto its cycle, the data trace the same closed loop again and again. On that loop, many different formulas agree, so the library becomes nearly redundant. With thirty minutes on the cycle, the law was found in none of forty draws. Six runs from six starting mixtures fill the space around the loop, fast starts included. Same noise, same method: thirty-nine out of forty. The same holds below the clock's threshold. With less of the second chemical, the mixture settles to a steady state. One run that started close to that steady state never found the law. Six starts found it twenty-eight times in forty. Discovery needs states that disagree with each other. Plan experiments that push the system into places the equation must explain. Real experiments rarely run one setting. Suppose we ran the clock at three feeds of the second chemical, b equal to 1.5, 2.5 and 3. Each run obeys its own law, but we suspect that one law covers them all, with the feed b inside it. So we give the library a second copy of every term, multiplied by b. Twenty candidates per equation. The search returned: dX by dt equals one, minus X, minus b times X, plus X squared Y. And dY by dt equals b times X, minus X squared Y. That's the Brusselator, with the feed in the right places, found in all forty draws. One equation now describes three regimes, including one where the clock doesn't tick at all. And a law with the feed inside it can be asked about feeds nobody ran. That's where the next video starts.

transcript.title: Recap
transcript.text: Let's recap. Derivatives are inferred objects. Finite differences, smoothing and weak forms each assume something, and those assumptions can fail even with perfect data. Sparse regression turns the search for terms into a fast linear problem, and its threshold should work across a wide window. Trajectory matching gives the best numbers, once you know the terms and have a good start. And the data must cover the space: many starting states, several settings, and the parameters written into the library. In the lab, you'll run this loop on the clock yourself. Next video: beyond the fit. Hidden species, bifurcations, noise inside the system, delays and forcing.

episodes.title: Beyond the fit: structure, stability and the real world
episodes.hook: Two laws fit our chemical clock equally well. At a feed nobody ran, one predicts the period within a tenth of a minute; the other blows up, stops, or guesses.
episodes.takeaway: A law for X alone explains 20% of its rate; rebuilding the hidden species from its known chemistry recovered the law in 40 of 40 draws. The found law puts the onset of ticking at b = 2.00, like the truth, and at b = 4 predicts the period within a tenth of a minute, where a 20-term fit blew up, stopped or guessed. A detector 24 s late, or a pump left out of the library, keeps the search from ever finding the law.

transcript.title: Two laws, one stress test
transcript.text: Two laws for our chemical clock. One has five terms, the other twenty. On our data, the twenty-term law fits slightly better, and both say that the clock starts ticking when the feed b passes two. Now turn the feed up to four, beyond anything we ran. We refitted both laws on eight noise draws. Every time, the five-term law predicts a period within a tenth of a minute of the truth, 9.0 minutes. The twenty-term law blew up once, stopped ticking twice, and otherwise said anything from 6.9 to 9.2 minutes. A good fit is where a dynamical law starts, not where it ends. This video is about the tests beyond the fit. This is the second video of Module seven. Part one: hidden species and partial knowledge. Part two: steady states and bifurcations as tests. Part three: noise inside the system, delays and inputs. Part four: a worked study, end to end.

transcript.title: Hidden species
transcript.text: Part one: hidden species. Suppose only X has a colour, and Y is invisible to our instrument. Pause here. Can any law for X alone, using only X, reproduce the clock? We tried: a law for the rate of X built from X and its powers up to five. It explains 20 percent of how X changes. With Y in the library, the same rates are explained to 99.96 percent. There's a reason. A law in one variable can only push a state up or down a line. It can never bring it back around. An oscillation needs at least two variables, so a hidden one must exist. Picture X as a bead on a wire. At each position, the law gives it one speed, with one sign. So the bead can only slide one way, or stop. To come back around, it would have to pass the same point moving the other way, and with one variable, it can't. With no knowledge of Y at all, there is another route: use X from a moment ago as a stand-in for the hidden variable. That can reproduce the motion, but the formula is written in borrowed coordinates, and its terms no longer read as chemistry. Partial knowledge helps. Suppose the chemistry of Y is known: it's made from X at rate b, and used up by the step that makes X. That gives dY by dt equals b X minus X squared Y, a law we can run with the measured X as its input. Start that law from a wrong guess, and the error fades. Y's equation forgets where it started. From a guess of zero, or of five, the rebuilt Y was within one percent of the truth after about six minutes. Better still, we know how much Y we poured in at the start. With that, rebuilding Y and running the search found the law for X in forty draws out of forty, with every coefficient within 0.1 percent. Hidden variables don't end discovery. But the knowledge that fills them in, here the chemistry of Y, becomes part of the claim, and it must be stated.

transcript.title: Steady states and bifurcations
transcript.text: Part two: structure as a test. A law makes promises the fit never checked. Where does the mixture stand still? Is that resting point stable? And at what feed does the clock begin to tick? Set both rates of the found law to zero. The steady state is X equal to one, and Y equal to b. At a feed of 2.5, the found law puts it at 1.00 and 2.50, right where the chemistry puts it. Then linearize around it. The eigenvalues of the Jacobian say whether small disturbances die out or grow. As b rises, a pair of complex eigenvalues crosses into growth at b equal to 2.00, for the found law and for the truth. That's a Hopf bifurcation: a steady state gives way to a cycle. The onset is an experiment you can run: raise the feed slowly, and note where the colour starts to swing. Both of our laws passed that test, because both were fitted on feeds on either side of it. Why does a pair of complex eigenvalues mean a clock? Near the steady state, the mixture moves in a spiral. While the pair's real part is negative, the spiral winds inward, and the colour settles. Once it turns positive, the spiral winds outward until it reaches a closed loop, and the colour keeps swinging. So we traced the whole diagram: the swing of X after settling, for feeds from one to four and a half. The truth and the five-term law overlap everywhere. The twenty-term law tracks them across the feeds we ran. Beyond them it drifts, blows up at 3.5, and from 3.75 on says the clock stops, while the real one keeps swinging wider. Steady states, stability and bifurcations are strong tests, because the fit never aimed at them. A law that passes them, outside the data too, has earned some trust. These tests run on the law alone, so they're cheap. Find every steady state, check its stability, compare the onsets with experiments, and look for cycles where the data had none.

transcript.title: Noise, delays and inputs
transcript.text: Part three: the real world. So far, the reaction was exact, and only our instrument was noisy. In a tiny droplet, the reaction itself is random. Molecules meet by chance, one at a time. Then there are two laws in the data: the average push, called the drift, and the size of the random kicks, called the diffusion. In a big beaker, with twenty thousand molecules per unit of concentration, six runs still gave the law in five noise draws out of six. In a droplet a hundred times smaller, the same search kept fourteen to twenty terms, even with thirty-six runs. But the kicks carry information too. Their size grows with the reaction rates, and fitting that relation put the droplet at about 180 to 210 molecules per unit. The truth is 200. So in a small system, the noise is more than a nuisance to average away. Its size is a measurement in its own right. Delays are another trap. Suppose the detector for X responds 24 seconds late. Ignore that, and the search keeps all twenty terms. Scan the assumed delay, and the fit error is smallest at 0.4 minutes, which is 24 seconds, where the law comes back in nine draws out of ten. Why so many terms? X arrives late, so each of its readings sits next to a Y from a different moment. No short law links the two, so the search piles up terms to bend one onto the other. And inputs. Suppose a pump varies the feed of the first chemical over a five-minute cycle. A library without the pump can't represent that: the search keeps nine terms for X and never finds the law. Add the pump's signal, u, as a candidate, and the law comes back in twenty draws of twenty: dX by dt equals u, minus 3.5 X, plus X squared Y. Delays, inputs and hidden states are part of the system. If the library can't express them, the search will invent something else to fill the gap.

transcript.title: A worked study, end to end
transcript.text: Part four: the whole study, end to end. Six starting mixtures at each of three feeds, a reading every three seconds, one percent noise. The weak form, a library with the feed inside it, and a threshold from a wide, stable window. The result is the Brusselator, found in all forty draws, with coefficients within about half a percent. Then the checks that the fit never saw. The steady state sits at one and b. The clock starts ticking at b equal to two. And at b equal to four, outside the data, the period is within a tenth of a minute of the true nine. And the report states it all: the data and how they were taken, the library, the threshold window, the steady-state and onset checks, the feeds where the law was tested, and what was assumed to be known. The weakest link is coverage. We ran feeds from 1.5 to 3. Outside that range, only the single check at four backs the law up, and the report should say so.

transcript.title: Recap
transcript.text: Let's recap. Hidden variables can be rebuilt when part of the system is known, and that knowledge becomes part of the claim. Steady states, stability and bifurcations are tests the fit never aimed at. A law should pass them before it's trusted outside the data. Noise inside the system, delays and inputs each need a place in the model. Otherwise the search fills the gap with terms that don't exist. In the lab, you'll break the clock and repair it yourself. Next module: laws in space and time, from partial differential equations to graphs.

episodes.title: Laws in space and time
episodes.hook: Watching one front pass a 40-km stretch of coast, a law-finding search wrote a drift that isn't there. A release in the middle gave the true law.
episodes.takeaway: At 1 km spacing the true curvature of the cover profile was five times smaller than the noise of its three-point estimate; finite differences never found the law, while the weak form found it in 20, 20 and 19 of 20 draws at 0.2, 0.5 and 1% noise, and in none at 2%.
