Total cover matched summed growth within 0.6%, and on two merging releases the true three-term law forecast best; a cubic term fit slightly better and forecast worse.

transcript.title: A plant on the coast
transcript.text: A plant is spreading along a hundred kilometres of coast. Sensors every kilometre report how much of the ground it covers, four times a week. We simulated it, added one percent noise, and gave a law-finding search the readings from a forty-kilometre stretch while one front passed through. It wrote five terms, including a drift, as if a wind were pushing the plant along the coast. Nineteen noise draws out of twenty included that drift. Then we released the same plant in the middle of the coast and gave the search the whole coast from the start. Three terms: growth, crowding and spread. The law we simulated, in nineteen draws out of twenty. Same plant, same law, same noise. What changed was what the data saw. This video is about laws in space and time. This is Module eight: partial differential equations, fields and graphs. Part one: fields and their noisy derivatives. Part two: libraries and the weak form in space and time. Part three: initial and boundary conditions as evidence. Part four: conservation. Part five: choosing among plausible laws.

transcript.title: A field and its law
transcript.text: A field is a quantity with a value at every place and every time. Here, u is the fraction of ground the plant covers, between zero and one, at each point along the coast, in each week. The law we simulated is a classic. The rate of change of u equals 0.5 times u times one minus u, plus 4 times the second derivative of u in space. The first part is growth that slows as the ground fills up. The second is spread: plant moves from crowded stretches into empty ones. Laws like this make fronts that travel. Theory says the front's speed settles at 2.8 kilometres a week. Over our 24 weeks, the front averaged 2.5, still speeding up toward that limit. Before any search, look at what the field shows. The release flattens and widens. Two fronts move apart at the same speed. And after about twenty-one weeks, they reach the closed ends of the coast, where nothing leaves. Where does 2.8 come from? At the leading edge, the plant is sparse, so crowding hardly matters yet. There, growth and spread alone set the pace, and the speed works out to twice the square root of the growth rate times the spread rate: twice the square root of 0.5 times 4.

transcript.title: Derivatives in a field
transcript.text: Part one: derivatives in a field. The law needs the second derivative in space, the curvature of the cover profile. With a sensor every kilometre, the simplest estimate takes three neighbouring readings: left plus right, minus twice the middle. At week twelve, the largest true curvature anywhere on the coast was 0.005 per square kilometre. With one percent noise, the error of that three-point estimate was 0.023. The noise is five times the biggest signal. The signal is small because the profile bends gently over many kilometres, while the noise of three readings adds up. Finite differences failed at every noise level we tried, even at 0.2 percent. In a field, the derivative problem from Module five comes back stronger: more derivatives, and higher ones.

transcript.title: Libraries and the weak form
transcript.text: Part two: libraries and the weak form. Our library has seven candidate terms. Cover, its square and its cube, for growth and crowding. The first derivative in space, for drift. The second, for spread. Cover times its first derivative, for transport that depends on cover. And a third derivative, which appears in some wave equations. The weak form now works in two directions. Take a window, twelve kilometres by three weeks. Multiply the law by a smooth bump that vanishes at the window's edges, and integrate. Integration by parts moves every derivative, in space and in time, onto the bump, which we know exactly. On the middle release at one percent noise, it returned the growth term, 0.50 u; the crowding term, minus 0.50 u squared; and 3.99 times the second derivative, for the spread. Each weight within one percent of the truth. What's left are integrals of the readings themselves, which average the noise. Across twenty noise draws, the weak form found the law every time at 0.2 percent noise, every time at 0.5 percent, and nineteen times at one percent. It has a limit. At two percent noise it failed too, every time. Past that point, the fix is better data: more sensors, or more frequent readings. A weak form doesn't make noise disappear. It moves the derivatives to where we know them exactly. There's a second gift. Every window gives one equation, and a coast watched for twenty-four weeks holds many windows, so the search sees the same law tested in many places and times at once.

transcript.title: Initial and boundary conditions as evidence
transcript.text: Part three: initial and boundary conditions are evidence. Back to the opening puzzle. Why did one front, crossing a forty-kilometre stretch, produce a drift? Pause and predict. A front that keeps its shape and moves at a steady speed: which law explains it, growth with spread, or pure drift? Both. A shape sliding at a steady speed satisfies the drift law exactly. Inside that window, the front was close to sliding, so drift and spread could explain the same readings, and the search mixed them. The release in the middle broke the tie. A bump of plant spreads both ways at once, and no single drift can explain that. Two fronts moving apart, a peak that flattens, and closed ends where nothing leaves: each is a place where the candidate laws disagree. Where an experiment starts, and where its edges are, are part of the data. Choose them so that the laws you're comparing must disagree. In practice, ask for the parts of an experiment that look boring: how it starts, what happens at the edges, the moment two fronts meet. Those are where a wrong law gets caught.

transcript.title: Conservation
transcript.text: Part four: conservation. Many field laws share one shape: the change at a place equals what flows in, minus what flows out, plus what's made there. Spread is a flow. Growth is making. That gives a check that needs no derivative of the field at all. With closed ends, flow only moves plant around. So the total cover along the coast can change only through growth. We checked it on the middle release. At every reading but the first and the last, the rate of change of the total matched the growth summed along the coast to within 0.6 percent of its peak. This splits the library in two. Terms that only move plant should be written as differences of a flow, so they sum to zero over a closed coast. Only growth terms may change the total. Building that split into the library removes candidates before the search begins. Conservation is a law about the law. Check it on the data, then build it into the library.

transcript.title: Choosing among plausible laws
transcript.text: Part five: choosing among plausible laws. We fitted four candidates to the middle release, then asked each to predict a new experiment: two releases, at 25 and 75 kilometres, whose fronts run into each other. Growth with spread: fit error 0.046, forecast error 0.002 of cover. Add a cubic growth term, and the fit gets slightly better, 0.045, while the forecast gets slightly worse, 0.003. Drift with growth fits four times worse, and misses the merger by 0.6. Spread with growth that never slows misses by about as much: 0.6 again. The cubic term's weight was 0.01, small enough to look harmless. It bought a better fit and a worse forecast. Choose among laws with experiments they haven't seen, designed where they disagree. Fit error alone always rewards an extra term.

transcript.title: Recap
transcript.text: Let's recap. A field law needs derivatives in space and time, and the higher ones drown in noise. The weak form moves them onto a bump we know exactly. Initial and boundary conditions decide which laws the data can tell apart. One front sliding through a window can't separate drift from spread. Conservation gives a check without derivatives, and a cleaner library. And between plausible laws, held-out experiments decide, not the fit. In the lab, you'll choose the experiment, the noise and the method, and see which laws survive. Next video: what if there's no grid at all? Laws on graphs.

episodes.title: From grids to graphs
episodes.hook: Offered a one-week delay, the search took it in 20 noise draws out of 20, and the fit improved. The simulation has no delay.
episodes.takeaway: On forty ponds the lowest fit error came from the graph we simulated with in 20 of 20 draws; it forecast a new introduction within a median 0.75 weeks, while nearest-neighbour graphs missed by 11.5 and 14.5 weeks. A one-week delay improved the fit and was chosen every time at 1% noise, never with cleaner data, and forecast 3.25 weeks off. The law transferred to a new map within 0.75 weeks, and the coupled plant and beetle laws went from 11 and 12 of 20 draws to 20 and 20 with a second run.

transcript.title: A delay nobody put in
transcript.text: We gave a law-finding search one extra option: a delay. Spread between ponds could depend on what the neighbours looked like a week earlier. The search took that option in twenty noise draws out of twenty, and the fit improved. There is no delay in the simulation we made. In part three, you'll see where it came from, and how a forecast caught it when the fit didn't. This video is about laws without a grid: laws on graphs. This is Module eight, video two. Part one: from grids to graphs. Part two: building the graph. Part three: edges in time. Part four: one law, many maps. Part five: coupled fields. And part six: benchmarks you can trust.

transcript.title: From grids to graphs
transcript.text: Our plant now lives in forty ponds, scattered over a landscape sixty kilometres on a side. Seeds travel between ponds. There's no coastline and no x axis, so there's no second derivative to take. On a graph, spread is a sum over neighbours: each neighbour's cover minus mine, times the weight of the edge between us. It's the graph's version of the second derivative, and it's called the graph Laplacian. We simulated growth at 0.5 per week, as before. Spread runs at the same rate, along edges whose weight fades with distance, falling by a factor of e every five kilometres, with no edges beyond fifteen. Two introductions, one in a corner and one in the middle. Readings four times a week, with one percent noise. Each pond gives its own time series, so the weak form works in time only. The library: cover, cover squared, and the graph term. Why does a sum over neighbours act like a second derivative? On a line of sensors, the sum over the two neighbours, left minus me plus right minus me, is exactly the three-point estimate from the last video: left plus right, minus twice the middle. A graph just lets the neighbours be anywhere.

transcript.title: Building the graph
transcript.text: Part two: building the graph. A law on a graph doesn't come with edges. We choose them, and the choice is part of the model. We tried seven: three or six nearest neighbours, every pond within eight or within fifteen kilometres, and weights that fade over two and a half, five or ten kilometres. Pause and predict. Which graph will forecast better: each pond linked to its six nearest neighbours, or every pond within fifteen kilometres, counted equally? The fit first. In all twenty noise draws, the lowest fit error came from the graph we simulated with, fading over five kilometres. Nearest-neighbour graphs fit worst. Then the real test: a third introduction, near another corner, and the week each pond reaches half cover. The five-kilometre graph missed by a median of 0.75 weeks. Within fifteen kilometres: 1.25. Six nearest neighbours: eleven and a half weeks. And within eight kilometres, the graph broke into islands, and the forecast reached three ponds out of thirty-nine. A nearest-neighbour graph gives a pond in a tight cluster the same number of links as an isolated pond, however far its neighbours are. In our landscape, spread depends on distance, not on how many neighbours a pond has. One honest caveat. Weights fading over ten kilometres forecast as well: a median of half a week. Forecasts couldn't separate those two graphs, while the fit preferred five kilometres every time. Report both. A useful habit: when the edges are a choice, keep the rejected graphs in the report. A reader who sees that six nearest neighbours missed by eleven and a half weeks learns how much the edge rule matters.

transcript.title: Edges in time
transcript.text: Part three: edges in time. Some processes really do have delays, like seeds that take a week to sprout. A temporal edge links the neighbours' cover a week ago to a pond's change now. So we added a week-old copy of the graph term to the library. The fit error dropped to 0.133, down from 0.147. And sparse regression kept the week-old copy and dropped the instant one, in all twenty draws. Then the forecast: arrival weeks off by a median of 3.25 weeks, instead of 0.75. A better fit, and a worse law. Where did the delay come from? The noise. With clean data, the search never picked it. At 0.2 and 0.5 percent noise, never. At one percent, every time. Noise also bends the instant term. On clean data, the spread rate comes out at 0.50. At one percent noise, it comes out at 0.42. A likely reason the week-old copy won: its noise is independent of today's readings, so it escapes part of that bias. So before believing a delay, run the same pipeline on simulated data with no delay and your noise level. If a delay appears there too, it's the pipeline talking, not the system.

transcript.title: One law, many maps
transcript.text: Part four: one law, many maps. A law written per pond and per edge isn't tied to these forty ponds. It's a rule for any map of ponds. So we drew a new landscape, forty other ponds, and ran the laws found on the first map, each with its own rule for edges. The five-kilometre law forecast arrival weeks within a median of 0.75 weeks, at all forty ponds. Within fifteen kilometres: 1.5 weeks. Six nearest neighbours reached thirty-five ponds of forty, and missed by eleven weeks. In machine learning, models that learn maps from one whole field to another, whatever the grid, are called neural operators. A symbolic law on a graph is a small, readable relative. It transfers because the edge rule is part of the law. An irregular domain isn't an obstacle for a graph law. The test is whether the law, edge rule included, works on a map it has never seen.

transcript.title: Coupled fields
transcript.text: Part five: coupled fields. Back to the coast, now with a beetle that eats the plant. There are two fields now, each with its own law. The plant grows, spreads, and is eaten, at a rate of u times v. The beetle spreads, grows by eating, 0.6 u v, and dies at 0.2 per week. Each law gets a library of seven terms: u and v, their squares, their product, and both second derivatives. One run: plant everywhere at 0.9 cover, beetles released in the middle. The plant's law came out right in eleven draws out of twenty, the beetle's in twelve. Here's a wrong beetle law: the right three terms, and two extras. Plus 0.01 u. And minus 0.01 u squared. Two tiny terms that nearly cancel. With the plant near 0.9 almost everywhere, u and u squared move together; their correlation was 0.994. The library can't tell them apart. The fix is the one that worked for the chemical clock: data where each field varies on its own. We added a second run that starts with sparse cover, five percent along the coast plus a dense patch at the west end, so the plant ranges from 0.05 to full cover. With both runs, both laws came out right in all twenty draws. In a coupled system, every field must move on its own somewhere in the data, or the search can swap a term for a look-alike.

transcript.title: Benchmarks you can trust
transcript.text: Part six: benchmarks you can trust. Every number in this module came with its noise level and its number of draws: twenty noise draws for each search, ten for each forecast. We reported the failures with the successes: the weak form at two percent noise, nearest-neighbour graphs, the eight-kilometre graph, the delay. And every claim was tested on an event the fit never saw: merging fronts, a third introduction, a new landscape. One more thing made these numbers checkable: we knew the true law, because we simulated it. With real data you won't. So before trusting a pipeline on real fields, run it on simulated fields with your sensors, your sampling and your noise, and see what it finds. A benchmark you can trust says what was tried, how often it worked, how it failed, and what it was tested on.

transcript.title: Recap
transcript.text: Let's recap. On a graph, spread becomes a sum over neighbours, and the edges are part of the model: choose them with the fit and with forecasts. A delay that appears in a found law may come from the noise. A negative control on simulated data tells you. A law with an edge rule transfers to new maps. Coupled fields need data where each field varies on its own. And benchmarks report draws, failures and held-out tests. In the lab, you'll choose the data, the method and the threshold, and test the law you find on an experiment it hasn't seen. Next module: trustworthy discovery. How sure can we be of a law we found?

episodes.title: How sure are we?
episodes.hook: A tank's law came with error bars. In 200 simulated experiments, the usual pipeline's 90% bars held the truth only 12.5% of the time.
episodes.takeaway: Nominal 90% intervals for the power covered the truth in 12.5% of 200 experiments with finite differences, 20% after smoothing, and 90% when fitting whole trajectories. Only the combination c = Cd·(a/A)·√(2g) reaches the data; a 40-second drain leaves the power anywhere from 0.19 to 0.84, and 79 different functions fit it. On a full drain, 61 formulas fit as well as the truth, all of them √h written differently.

transcript.title: Error bars that aren't
transcript.text: A tank of water drains through a small hole, and a sensor reads the level every two seconds, to the millimetre. A fit gives the law: the level falls at a rate proportional to the level to a power. The fitted power is 0.5005, give or take 0.0006. But how sure is that? We repeated the experiment two hundred times in simulation, with fresh noise each time, and checked how often the ninety-percent error bars of three common pipelines contained the true power, one half. Finite differences with a log-log fit: twelve percent of the time. Smoothing first: twenty percent. Fitting whole trajectories: ninety percent, as promised. Same data, same tank. Only the pipeline differed. An error bar is a claim too, and it can be wrong. This video is about how sure we can be. This is Module nine: trustworthy equation discovery. Part one: the sources of uncertainty. Part two: calibrating error bars. Part three: identifiability, when the data can't decide. Part four: when different formulas mean the same thing.

transcript.title: A draining tank
transcript.text: Our tank is a cylinder with a cross-section of five hundred square centimetres, draining through a one-centimetre hole. Torricelli worked out the law in the sixteen-forties: water leaves the hole as fast as if it had fallen from the surface, so the level drops at a rate proportional to the square root of the level. From a full metre, our tank empties in about eight minutes. We simulated three drains, from one metre, seventy centimetres and forty centimetres, with one millimetre of sensor noise. The sensor stops below two centimetres, so a drain from one metre gives two hundred and six readings, one every two seconds. We wrote the law as: the rate of fall equals a constant c times the level to a power p, and let the fit find both. The truth is p equals one half. The constant c depends on the hole and on the tank. We'll come back to it in part three. One consequence you can see by eye: the tank slows down as it empties. From a full metre, the level falls to half a metre in only about thirty percent of the drain time. The last half metre takes the other seventy.

transcript.title: Sources of uncertainty
transcript.text: Part one: where uncertainty comes from. First, noise: the sensor's millimetre. Second, the parameters: the same data allow a range of constants. Third, the structure: other formulas may fit as well. And fourth, the pipeline: how we estimate derivatives, which library, which threshold. Each needs its own check. Noise and parameters give error bars. Structure needs competing laws. And the pipeline needs the same analysis run several ways, which is the next video's subject. Many reports give only the second. A trustworthy one names all four, and says which were checked. For our tank: the noise is one millimetre. The error on the power, fitted on three drains, is 0.0006. One rival law, a rate that is a straight line in the level, fits the first minute and a half as well as Torricelli's law. And changing the pipeline alone moved the power by three hundredths. A single number with a single error bar covers only the first two.

transcript.title: Calibrating error bars
transcript.text: Part two: calibration. A ninety-percent interval should contain the truth in nine experiments out of ten. That's checkable, if you can repeat the experiment, or simulate it. The finite-difference pipeline takes differences of neighbouring readings, then fits a straight line on a log-log plot. Its power came out at 0.53, biased, and its intervals contained one half in only twelve percent of the experiments. Smoothing first removed the bias, but the intervals were far too narrow, because the fit treats smoothed derivatives as independent measurements, which they're not. Twenty percent. Why does independence matter so much? Smoothing makes neighbouring derivatives share most of their noise. A fit that believes it has two hundred independent readings thinks it knows more than it does, and its interval shrinks to match. Fitting the solution of the law directly to the readings, where the noise really is independent, gave intervals that covered the truth in ninety percent of the experiments, and they were the narrowest of the three. The trajectory intervals were 1.8 thousandths wide. The smoothing ones were wider, 3.1 thousandths, and still too narrow: their estimates scattered over 16 thousandths, on both sides of one half. If you can't repeat the real experiment, simulate it: use your fitted law and your noise level to make many synthetic copies, refit each one, and count how often the intervals cover the law you simulated. Check your error bars the way you'd check a law: on data where you know the answer.

transcript.title: Identifiability
transcript.text: Part three: identifiability. The law's constant depends on three physical quantities: the discharge coefficient of the hole, the hole's area, and the tank's area. Only their combination reaches the data. Take three holes. The first has a coefficient of 0.6. The second has 0.8, and a slightly smaller diameter. The third has 0.48, and a larger one. The three tanks drain identically, to the last digit. No amount of level data can separate them. You'd need another measurement, like the size of the hole. The fix isn't a better fit. Either add a measurement that separates them, or report only the combination the data can see: here, the constant c, 0.0042. This is common in real systems. A rate constant and a concentration that only ever appear as a product, or a mass and a stiffness seen only through their ratio: the data see the combination, never the parts. That's structural non-identifiability. There's a practical kind too. Watch the tank for only forty seconds, a drop of sixteen centimetres, and the power could be anything from 0.19 to 0.84: from about a fifth to over four fifths. In that short window, the constant and the power trade against each other: a bigger power with a bigger constant draws almost the same curve. Their estimates were correlated at 0.96. Watch the whole drain, and the range shrinks to 0.499 to 0.501. Practical non-identifiability can be fixed with data: a longer drain, or drains from several levels, each pinning down the trade-off from a different side. When parameters trade off, the data haven't decided. Report the trade-off, or design data that break it.

transcript.title: When formulas mean the same thing
transcript.text: Part four: when different formulas mean the same thing. We asked a small search to try every formula of up to five symbols, built from the level, one, two, square roots, logs, exponentials and the four operations, each with one fitted constant: 1,629 formulas. Sixty-one of them fit the full drain as well as Torricelli's law, within two percent. All sixty-one are Torricelli's law: the square root of h, h over the square root of h, the square root of h plus h, the square root of the log of e to the h. One law, written sixty-one ways. Counting them as sixty-one discoveries would be wrong. Simplify, or compare the formulas numerically at many points, before you count. A practical test: after fitting their constants, evaluate two formulas at a few hundred random points, inside and outside the data range. If they agree everywhere to many digits, they are one law. A computer algebra system can often confirm it symbolically. The best formula that was really different, h plus the fourth root of h, fit 4.2 times worse than the truth. On the full drain, the data chose clearly. That's the pattern to look for. A wide gap between the best fit and the next different formula means the data have chosen. A crowd of near-ties means they haven't. Now the short, forty-second drain. Five hundred and ninety-two formulas fit it as well as the truth, and they are seventy-nine different functions. Near the bottom of the tank, at three centimetres, they disagree wildly: some even predict the level rising. Remember that the next time a search returns a surprising formula from a short experiment. Many formulas fitting the same data isn't a surprise. It's a measurement of how little the data say.

transcript.title: Recap
transcript.text: Let's recap. Uncertainty has four sources: noise, parameters, structure and pipeline. Each needs its own check. Error bars must be calibrated: on repeated or simulated experiments, a ninety-percent interval should cover the truth nine times in ten. Some combinations of parameters can never be separated by the data, and some only by better data. And formulas must be compared as functions, not as strings. In the lab, you'll stress-test a tank law yourself. Next video: robustness and honest validation.

episodes.title: Robustness and honest validation
episodes.hook: Twenty-one ways to analyse the same tank put the power between 0.488 and 0.531. That spread is part of the result.
episodes.takeaway: Across 21 pipelines the power stayed within 0.05 of 1/2, 19 within 0.02. Held out by range, the law missed by 1.3 mm and a polynomial by 59; with a bigger hole the polynomial blew up in 12 of 20 tries. A syrup gave p = 1.0001; shuffled readings still gave the log-log pipeline a power, while the trajectory fit's error rose to 229 mm.

transcript.title: Twenty-one pipelines, one tank
transcript.text: We took one tank and one kind of data, and analysed them twenty-one ways: three ways to estimate derivatives, two ways to fit, and three slices of the data, plus fitting whole trajectories. The lowest power was 0.488. The highest was 0.531. All twenty-one were within 0.05 of one half; nineteen within 0.02. The two outliers share one choice: differences of noisy neighbours, fitted on a log-log plot. Each pipeline ran on twenty noise draws, on each of the three slices; the numbers here are the medians. Twenty-one numbers, one tank. A result that survives many reasonable pipelines is a robust result. This video is about testing a law as if you meant it. This is Module nine, video two. Part one: robustness across pipelines. Part two: splits that match the claim. Part three: interpolation is not discovery. Part four: distribution shift. Part five: baselines, negative controls and ablations.

transcript.title: Robustness across pipelines
transcript.text: Part one. A pipeline is every choice between the raw readings and the reported law: derivatives, smoothing, library, threshold, fitting method, and which data were kept. Each choice is reasonable; none is the only option. So run several. If the law appears in most reasonable pipelines, report that, with the spread. If it appears in only one, then that choice is the result, not the tank. A practical way to do this: write the pipeline once, with each choice as a setting, then run every combination you would be willing to defend. The table of results is the robustness check. Running many pipelines isn't hiding behind an average. If they disagree, the disagreement is itself a finding: the data alone don't settle the question. In our table, nineteen pipelines agreed to within 0.02, and that agreement is what we can stand behind. Here, the spread itself was informative. Both outliers took logs of noisy differences of neighbouring readings, which distorts small rates the most, near the bottom of the tank. That's the most likely source of their bias. The slice of data mattered too. On the top half of the tank alone, the pipelines leaned low: the lowest was 0.488. On the bottom half, they leaned high: the highest was 0.525. Trajectory fitting gave 0.500 on all three slices. Robustness is a distribution over pipelines, not a single run.

transcript.title: Splits that match the claim
transcript.text: Part two: the split must match the claim. Our claim: this law describes the tank from any starting level, and for any small hole. So we compared it with a flexible rival: a degree-four polynomial in the level. Matching the split to the claim isn't extra rigour. It's what the claim means: any starting level means testing a level you didn't train on. Hold out random readings, and both do fine: one millimetre for the law, 1.3 for the polynomial. Hold out a whole drain from a new starting level inside the range: 1.2 and 1.4. Now a split that matches the claim. Train above forty centimetres, and predict a drain from thirty. The law: 1.3 millimetres. The polynomial: fifty-nine, and three times out of twenty its forecast blew up. Why? Inside the range, five numbers can bend a polynomial along any smooth curve. Outside it, nothing ties the polynomial to the physics: even at an empty tank, its rate isn't zero. Torricelli's law has that limit built in. At zero level, the square root is zero, so the outflow stops. The polynomial's constant term doesn't know the tank exists. And a bigger hole. The law refits one number, its constant, from the first twenty seconds, and predicts the rest within 1.5 millimetres. The polynomial refits all five of its numbers from the same twenty seconds; its forecast blew up in twelve tries out of twenty. Why such a difference? One number is easy to pin down in twenty seconds. Five numbers aren't: many combinations fit a short stretch equally well, and they disagree wildly as soon as the data run out. Two splits looked alike for both models; two others separated them completely. Only the second kind tests the claim we wanted to make. A random split tests interpolation. If you claim more, test more.

transcript.title: Interpolation is not discovery
transcript.text: Part three: interpolation is not discovery. A degree-eight polynomial in time fits our one-metre drain to 0.99 millimetres, as well as the noise allows. But it knows nothing about tanks. Ask it about a minute after the last reading, and it says eighteen millimetres; two minutes after, eighteen centimetres: a tank that refills itself. And it can't say anything about a drain from another level, because the level isn't in it. Notice what made the polynomial in time fail. Its variable is the clock, not the state of the tank. A law in the level carries over to any start, because the level is what the water responds to. Many flexible models behave like this: excellent between the data points, silent or wrong beyond them. A law earns the name by working where it wasn't fitted. A neural network trained on these readings would face the same question: what does it say about a level, a hole or a fluid it never saw? A formula that only reproduces the data it saw is a summary, not a law.

transcript.title: Distribution shift
transcript.text: Part four: distribution shift. Change the conditions the law will meet, and see what happens. A hole of 1.4 centimetres, almost twice the area: the power stayed at 0.4995, and the constant grew by 1.96, the area ratio. With the bigger hole, a full tank empties in about four minutes instead of eight. We chose these shifts by asking what a user of the law would change: the hole, and the fluid. Now a thick syrup through a long, thin outlet. The flow is slow and smooth, and physics expects a different law: a rate of fall proportional to the level itself. The same pipeline found a power of 1.0001. Why a power of one for the syrup? In slow, smooth flow through a long, thin outlet, the flow rate is proportional to the pressure that drives it, and that pressure is proportional to the level. That's not a failure. The pipeline worked, and the law changed with the fluid. Torricelli's law, forced onto the syrup, missed by thirty-eight millimetres. A law comes with a domain, and shift tests find its edges. A shift that breaks the law is still a result: it marks where the claim stops. Stress tests should include the conditions under which you expect the law to break.

transcript.title: Baselines, controls and ablations
transcript.text: Part five: baselines, negative controls and ablations. Baselines first. On the held-out low drain, Torricelli's law missed by 1.2 millimetres. A constant rate: seventy-three. An exponential decay: sixty-four. The polynomial: fifty-nine. Baselines should be strong: the best simple model a sceptic would propose, not a straw man that any law beats. A negative control is data where the answer should be nothing. We shuffled the readings in time. The log-log pipeline still reported a power, 0.07, with an error bar. The trajectory fit refused to look good: its error jumped to 229 millimetres. Why did the log-log pipeline report a number at all? It fits a line through whatever points it gets, and its error bar measures only the scatter around that line. It never asks whether the line means anything. A positive control is data with a known, different answer: the syrup. The pipeline found it, as it should. Negative controls catch pipelines that always find something. Positive controls catch pipelines that can't find anything new. And ablations remove one ingredient at a time. Drop the readings below half a metre, and the uncertainty of the power grew thirteen-fold. Swap trajectory fitting for finite differences, and the bias came back. An ablation that changes nothing is useful too. It tells you which parts of the pipeline the result doesn't depend on, and which ones it does. Every claim deserves a rival, a control that should fail, and an ablation that shows what each part contributes.

transcript.title: Recap
transcript.text: Let's recap. Run many reasonable pipelines, and report the spread. Make the split match the claim: new starting levels, new ranges, new holes. Random rows test only interpolation. Fitting what you saw isn't discovery. Shift tests find a law's domain. And baselines, negative and positive controls, and ablations keep the claim honest. And report every test, including the ones a law failed. Next video: falsification, reproducibility, and people in the loop.

episodes.title: Falsification, reproducibility and people in the loop
episodes.hook: Two laws fit the first 106 seconds of a draining tank equally well. One 60-second run from 10 cm falsified the rival.
episodes.takeaway: From 10 cm, the rivals' forecasts missed by 28 and 25 mm, Torricelli's by 1.4. A closed loop needed one experiment every time; random choices needed two on average and up to eight. One changed default moved the power from 0.500 to 0.531, more than ten noise seeds did.

transcript.title: Which experiment tells them apart?
transcript.text: We watched our tank fall from one metre to sixty centimetres, a minute and three quarters. Torricelli's law fits that stretch to 0.9 millimetres. So does a rival: a rate that's a straight line in the level. An exponential decay comes close. Which experiment tells them apart fastest? Starting a minute-long run from ninety centimetres, inside the stretch we'd seen, the laws differ by about one and a half noise widths. Starting from ten centimetres, by seventeen. We ran it: Torricelli's law missed by 1.4 millimetres, the other two by twenty-eight and twenty-five. Falsified. The best next experiment is the one where your rival laws disagree most. This video is about falsification, reproducibility, and the people in the loop. This is the last video of Module nine. Part one: discriminating experiments. Part two: closing the loop. Part three: Pareto fronts with trust. Part four: reproducibility beyond code. Part five: people in the loop.

transcript.title: Discriminating experiments
transcript.text: Part one. Agreeing with data can't prove a law, but disagreeing can refute one. So design experiments that could refute a law, and better still, experiments that will refute one of the rivals, whichever is true. In 1964, John Platt called this strong inference: devise alternative hypotheses, then experiments that would exclude some of them. Platt's point was speed. A field that tests one favourite hypothesis at a time moves slowly. A field that pits alternatives against each other in every experiment moves fast. The training data were one drain, watched from one metre down to sixty centimetres. We tried ten starting levels, from ten centimetres to one metre, each for one minute. For each possible starting level, we predicted a minute of draining with each law, refitted on twenty noise draws to include their uncertainty, and scored how far apart the predictions were, in units of noise. Near the levels we'd already seen, the laws agree. The disagreement grows as the start gets lower, and peaks at ten centimetres. Down there, the exponential slows the fall far more than Torricelli's law, and the straight line far less. There's a simple reason. The rival laws were fitted to the same stretch, so they're forced to agree there. Away from it, nothing holds them together, and their differences grow. Discriminating doesn't mean extreme. Ten centimetres is an ordinary level for this tank. We just hadn't watched it yet. The most informative experiment is chosen before it's run, by asking where the laws disagree.

transcript.title: Closing the loop
transcript.text: Part two: closing the loop. A closed loop repeats this automatically: fit the surviving laws, choose the next experiment where they disagree most, forecast it before seeing it, drop any law whose forecast misses by more than five noise widths, refit, and repeat. We ran that loop twelve times from fresh noise. It settled on Torricelli's law after one experiment every time. Choosing the next starting level at random instead took two experiments on average, and up to eight. Neither loop ever dropped the true law. Why does choosing well help so much? A random start often lands near the levels already seen, where the laws still agree, and that run tells you almost nothing. Of the forty random loops, twenty-three settled after one experiment and nine after two; one took eight. Choosing well saved experiments, and in a real lab, experiments are the expensive part. The loop also knew when to stop: with one law left, there was nothing left to discriminate. In a closed loop, people set the rules, and the loop applies them without getting tired or hopeful. Automation raises the bar for verification. A loop that runs experiments on its own needs the same honesty as a person: forecasts recorded before results, a stated rule for dropping a law, and a log of every decision. A closed loop is falsification at machine speed. It's only as trustworthy as its rules.

transcript.title: Pareto fronts with trust
transcript.text: Part three: Pareto fronts with trust. Usually we plot complexity against error and pick a law on the front. But error isn't the only thing we care about. Fitted on all three drains, Torricelli's law, with one constant, misses by one millimetre. The power law with a free power: also one, with two constants. The degree-four polynomial: 1.2 millimetres, with five. The straight line: 6.7. A constant rate and an exponential: thirty-seven or more. Notice the power law with a free power. It fits as well as Torricelli's law, but its second constant only says one half. On the Pareto front, the simpler law dominates it. Now add trust columns. Does the law stop at an empty tank? Torricelli's does: its rate goes to zero with the level. The straight line keeps falling below zero; the exponential never empties at all; and the polynomial's rate at an empty tank isn't zero either. These are checks you can run without a single new reading: put the level to zero in each formula, and ask what happens. And stability. Refitted on twelve noise draws, Torricelli's law put the empty time at 479 seconds, within 0.2. The polynomial said 448, with a spread of five seconds. The truth is 479. A trust column can be anything you would otherwise check by hand: units, limits, symmetries, and whether the law survived the stress tests of the last video. Here the trust columns didn't change the winner; they explained why it wins. When they do change the winner, that's worth knowing before you publish. Put physical sense and stability next to error and complexity, and the choice usually becomes obvious.

transcript.title: Reproducibility beyond code
transcript.text: Part four: reproducibility beyond code. Same readings, same code, one setting changed. Differences of neighbours on a log-log plot: 0.531. Smooth over eleven readings first: 0.502. Over forty-one: 0.501. Fit trajectories: 0.500. Sharing the code isn't enough if a default changes between versions. Record the data version, every setting, the random seeds and the software versions. And report how much the answer moves with the noise itself: across ten noise seeds, it stayed within a thousandth of one half: 0.4992 to 0.5005. A simple habit helps: save a short file next to every result, with the data version, the settings and the seeds, written by the same script that produced the number. In our tank, one changed default, from smoothing to plain differences, moved the answer more than the noise did across all ten seeds. We saw the same thing in Module five: the pipeline is part of the result, so it belongs in the report. Publish the data and the simulated checks too, not just the code, so others can rerun the calibration and the controls, not only the fit. Reproducible means another person, with your data and your record, gets your number.

transcript.title: People in the loop
transcript.text: Part five: people in the loop. Many checks in this module are judgement calls: which rivals are plausible, which controls should fail, which physical limits matter, like a rate that must vanish when the tank is empty. A person who knows tanks would reject the straight-line law on sight, whatever its fit. Build that knowledge in as explicit checks, and let people review what the search proposes, especially when an automated loop runs the experiments. Explicit checks also make the judgement visible. A rule that is written down, like a rate that must vanish at an empty tank, can be read, argued with and changed. A hunch can't. In this module, a person chose the rival laws, the syrup control, and the rule that a tank's rate must vanish when it's empty. None of those came from the data. And when a loop runs experiments on real equipment, a person should be able to stop it, see why it chose each experiment, and review every decision. The point isn't to slow the search down. It's to aim it: at plausible rivals, at controls that mean something, and at experiments worth running. Human oversight isn't a step after discovery. It belongs inside the loop.

transcript.title: Recap
transcript.text: Let's recap. Choose experiments where rival laws disagree, and forecast them before running them. A closed loop does this quickly, and needs explicit rules and records. Put trust on the Pareto front: physical sense and stability next to error and complexity. Record everything that can change a result. And keep people inside the loop. And design experiments that could prove you wrong. In the lab, you'll stress-test a tank law and choose the next experiment. Next module: extensions of symbolic regression.

episodes.title: Symbolic regression inside bigger AI systems
episodes.hook: Eight textbook laws, 160 trials: the best fit was right 131 times. A loop with three critics was right every time, after about two tool calls.
episodes.takeaway: With gravity nearly fixed, the best fit chose the wrong power of g in 15 of 20 water-pressure trials; one answer had the wrong units and missed wider data by 220%. The units critic cut the fits from about 144 to about 2 per task; either critic alone was enough here, but with only a fit check the loop was wrong 95 times in 160.

transcript.title: One-shot search or a loop?
transcript.text: We gave the same eight textbook laws to two procedures. Each law came with thirty noisy measurements from a narrow range. A one-shot search, which returns the formula that fits best, got 131 right, out of 160. A small loop, which proposes the simplest formula not yet tried, fits it, and lets three critics check it, got all 160 right, with about two tool calls per task. Same search space, same data. The difference was orchestration. This video is about symbolic regression inside bigger systems. This is Module ten, the last module: extensions of symbolic regression. Part one: interfaces. Part two: discovery as orchestration. Part three: mechanisms and agents. Part four: how to evaluate a discovery system.

transcript.title: Interfaces matter more than labels
transcript.text: Part one: interfaces matter more than labels. Call it a neural network, an agent or a genetic program: what matters is what goes in and what comes out. A good symbolic regression tool takes data with units and ranges, the knowledge you trust, and the claim you want to test. It returns not one formula, but candidates with their errors, their uncertainty, the tests they passed and failed, and a log of how they were found. Ranges matter as much as units. A formula is only claimed where it was tested, so a tool that reports the range of its data tells you where its answer stops. Logs matter more than they seem. A formula without its history can't be checked: you don't know how many candidates were tried, which data were used, or which tests it failed before one passed. That interface lets a bigger system use the tool: call it, check its answer, and call it again with a better question. In Module three, units were a rule inside the search. Here, they're a critic outside it. Whatever is inside, judge a discovery tool by what it promises at its edges.

transcript.title: Discovery as orchestration
transcript.text: Part two: orchestration rather than one-shot generation. Our eight tasks: a projectile's range, a pendulum's period, the speed of water from a hole, kinetic energy, a spring's period, drag, a centripetal force, and water pressure. Each had thirty measurements with two percent noise, in a narrow range, with gravity held near Earth's value. The search space was the same for both procedures: a constant times the inputs raised to powers from minus two to two, about three hundred candidates per task. Some tasks include an input that doesn't matter, like the pendulum's mass, to see whether the search leaves it out. The one-shot search picked the best fit, and in 29 of 160 cases that was wrong. For water pressure it was wrong fifteen times in twenty: with gravity nearly fixed, the data couldn't tell which power of gravity to use, and the noise chose for it. That's a general trap. When an input barely varies in the data, any power of it fits about equally well, so the fit can't choose. Only data where gravity changes, or a units check, can decide. One of its answers: the density squared, times the square root of gravity, times the depth. It fitted the narrow data as well as the law did. On wider data, including the Moon and Mars, it was off by 220 percent. And its units are wrong: anyone who checked them would have thrown it out. For the pendulum, one wrong answer dropped gravity altogether: a constant times the square root of the length. It missed the wider data by 37 percent. For the water from a hole, the same mistake missed by 93. The loop works differently. A proposer offers formulas, simplest first. A units critic rejects any formula whose units don't match, before fitting anything. A fit critic asks whether the error is within one and a half times the noise. And a range critic tests the survivor on thirty measurements from a wider range, from less than half to two and a half times the narrow one, with gravity on Earth, Mars and the Moon. The units critic is cheap and strict. Of the 343 candidate formulas for the pendulum, only one has units of seconds. For the range, eight have units of length, and the fit critic chose among them. Units checks are this strong because they don't depend on the data at all. A formula with the wrong units can fit one range by luck, but it can't be a law in every system of units. The loop found every law, with about two tool calls per task: one fit and one range check. Without the units critic, it still found them all, but needed about 144 tool calls per task. Without the range critic, it also found them all: in our tasks, either critic was enough on its own. Remove both, keeping only the fit check, and the loop went wrong in 95 of 160 cases. Simplest first isn't enough: in a narrow range, a simple wrong formula fits as well as the right one. An agent is a search with critics. The critics are where the science goes.

transcript.title: Mechanisms and agents
transcript.text: Part three: mechanisms and agents. A mechanistic agent goes further: it proposes mechanisms, not just formulas, and designs experiments to choose among them. We ran a small version in Module nine. The loop fitted three rival laws for a draining tank, chose the starting level where they disagreed most, forecast the result before seeing it, and dropped the laws that missed. One experiment was enough, every time. That loop had the same parts as today's: a proposer, critics, and a list of what had been ruled out. The new part was the experiment. Instead of judging candidates on the data it had, it chose the data that would judge them best. The list of what's been ruled out matters too. Without it, a proposer can suggest the same failed idea again in new words, and the loop pays for the same test twice. Language models can now take the proposer's seat: suggesting mechanisms, writing code, reading the literature. That makes the critics more important, not less. A fluent proposal is not evidence. A language model can propose a mechanism in a sentence, and write the code to fit it in a minute. It can also propose a mechanism that sounds right and isn't, or write code with a quiet bug. So its proposals get the same critics: units, fit to the noise, a wider range, and a designed experiment. Let anything propose. Let only evidence decide.

transcript.title: Evaluating discovery systems
transcript.text: Part four: how to evaluate a discovery system. First, tasks with known answers, and enough of them: we used eight laws, with twenty noise draws each. Twenty draws turn anecdotes into rates. Second, measure more than success. Count wrong answers separately from abstentions: a system that says I don't know is better than one that is confidently wrong. And count the cost: fits, experiments, time. Cost matters because some steps are cheap and some aren't. A units check costs nothing, a fit costs a little, and a new experiment can cost a week. Good loops spend the cheap checks first. Our loop could abstain: if no candidate passed all three critics, it would return nothing. Here, it never had to. On harder tasks, a good loop abstains more often, and that should count in its favour. Third, test outside the training range, as our range critic did, and report the failures task by task. Our one-shot search was perfect on four laws, and right only thirteen and five times in twenty on two others. Fourth, beware of memory. Textbook laws can be recognised rather than discovered, especially by systems trained on textbooks. Good benchmarks rename variables, change units, or use laws that no one has written down yet. And fifth, ablations. Remove each critic and count what breaks. Ours showed something we didn't expect: either critic alone was enough here, and the units critic was far cheaper. Only an ablation tells you which parts of a system are doing the work. A discovery system is a scientific instrument. Calibrate it before you trust it.

transcript.title: Recap
transcript.text: Let's recap. Interfaces matter more than labels: data, units and claims in; candidates, uncertainty, tests and logs out. Orchestration beats one-shot generation when the critics carry real knowledge: units, noise and range. Agents can propose mechanisms and experiments, but evidence must still decide. And evaluate discovery systems on known answers, with costs, abstentions, failures and ablations. Next video, the last of the course: distillation, symbolic features, generated data, and what comes next.

episodes.title: Distillation, symbolic features, generated data, and what's next
episodes.hook: A neural network learned a projectile's range to 2.6%. A symbolic student fitted to its answers wrote the textbook law, and was more accurate than its teacher.
episodes.takeaway: Distilled where the teachers learned, both students wrote R = v²·sin 2θ / g (0.4% and 0.7% off); distilled over wider speeds they copied their teachers' mistakes (40% and 70% off). A straight line on the found feature was 0.19% off, and 0.03% beyond the data; with 400 generated shots added to 40 real ones, the search found the law in 0 of 20 trials.

transcript.title: A formula from a black box
transcript.text: A neural network learned a projectile's range from four hundred noisy shots, with an error of 2.6 percent. Then we asked a symbolic student to imitate it. The student wrote: the range equals 0.1023 times the speed squared, times the sine of twice the angle. That's the textbook law, with one over g equal to 0.102. And the student was more accurate than its teacher. The student was 0.4 percent off. The teacher was 2.6 percent off. Distillation turns a black box into a formula you can read. This last video is about distillation, symbolic features, generated data, and what comes next. Part one: distilling a neural teacher. Part two: what a student explains, and distilling trees. Part three: symbolic regression as feature engineering. Part four: generated data. Part five: what's next.

transcript.title: Distilling a neural teacher
transcript.text: Our data: four hundred shots on flat ground without drag, at speeds from five to twenty metres per second and angles from ten to eighty degrees, with two percent noise. The law: the range equals the speed squared times the sine of twice the angle, over g. The teacher: a small neural network, two layers of thirty-two units, trained on the shots. The student: a constant, times a power of the speed, times one of eight functions of the angle, from a sine to a simple parabola. We asked the teacher two thousand questions inside its training range, and fitted the student to its answers. Why two thousand questions, when we only had four hundred shots? A teacher can be asked as often as we like, so the student gets as many answers as it needs, spread evenly over the range. The student matched its teacher to within 2.7 percent. It matched the truth to within 0.4. Why better than the teacher? The student's shape is restricted, so it can't follow the teacher's small wiggles. It keeps what the teacher learned that a formula can express, and drops the rest. And because the student's formula is the law, it was just as good at speeds from twenty to thirty metres per second, where the teacher had never seen a shot: 0.4 percent off there too. Fitted directly to the four hundred shots, the same student found the law too, even more precisely. So when you have the data, fit the data. Distil when you have the model but not the data: a published network, a simulator too slow to search, or a model trained on data you can't share. A good student isn't a copy. It's the part of the teacher that can be written down.

transcript.title: What a student explains
transcript.text: Part two: what a student explains. A student fitted to a teacher explains the teacher, not the world. Ask the network about speeds it never saw, from twenty to thirty metres per second, and its error grows to fourteen percent. Now ask the teacher over that wider range, and the student copies the teacher's mistakes. It wrote the speed to the power 1.5, times a parabola in the angle: forty percent off inside the original range, fourteen beyond it. The parabola looks a lot like the sine of twice the angle: both are zero at zero and ninety degrees, and both peak at forty-five. Given a teacher's slightly wrong answers, the student can't tell which one is the physics. They're close, not equal. Scaled to agree at forty-five degrees, at eighty degrees the parabola gives 0.40. The sine gives 0.34. A small gap, easily hidden by a teacher's errors. Gradient-boosted trees, three hundred small ones, make the point sharper. Their predictions are a staircase: 7.2 percent off inside the range, and flat beyond it, 39 percent off at the higher speeds. Trees can only predict values they've seen in training. Beyond the data, each tree returns the value of its outermost leaf, which is why the staircase goes flat. Distilled inside the range, the trees' student was the true law again, 0.7 percent off. Yet it matched its teacher only to 8.4 percent. Distilled over the wider range, it put the speed to the first power, and was seventy percent off inside the original range. So query the teacher where it learned from data, and nowhere else. And report fidelity, how well the student copies its teacher, separately from accuracy, how well it matches the world. Distillation can't add knowledge the teacher doesn't have. It can only make that knowledge readable.

transcript.title: Symbolic features
transcript.text: Part three: symbolic regression as feature engineering. A linear model on the raw speed and angle is forty-eight percent off. The same linear model on one found feature, the speed squared times the sine of twice the angle, is 0.19 percent off. At speeds it never saw, it is 0.03 percent off. That one feature did more than either black box: the trees were 7.2 percent off inside the range. The network was 2.6 percent off. And both were much worse beyond it. Why does it work? The hard part of the problem, how the range bends with speed and angle, is inside the feature. What's left for the model is a straight line. A straight line extrapolates well when the feature is right, and badly when it isn't. That suggests a modest way to use symbolic regression: not as the final model, but as a source of a few strong features for a model you already trust. A representation bank goes one step further: a list of candidate features, here eleven, and a sparse fit that chooses among them. With any threshold from 0.2 to 0.8, it kept exactly one: the speed squared times the sine of twice the angle. With lower thresholds, it kept four, all of them the speed squared times something. At 1.2, it kept nothing. The threshold is a choice, as it was for sparse regression earlier in the course: sweep it, and report what survives across the sweep. Symbolic features let simple models do the work of complex ones, and carry them beyond the data.

transcript.title: Generated data
transcript.text: Part four: generated data. Suppose we only had forty real shots. Could a generative model add more? We fitted a mixture of Gaussians to the forty shots, and drew four hundred new ones from it. With the forty real shots alone, the search found the law in all twenty trials, 0.3 percent off. With the four hundred generated shots added, it found the law in none, and was thirty-three percent off. Why so much worse? The search trusted every shot equally, and ten generated shots outnumbered each real one. The law had to fit the generator's version of the world. The real shots scattered about two percent around the law. A typical generated shot was nineteen percent off, and seven in ten were more than ten percent off: the generator copied the spread of the data, not the physics. One trial's answer was a parabola in the angle, with a constant that fitted the generator, not gravity. Larger generators, including diffusion models, are far better at looking realistic. The rule doesn't change: generated data carry the generator's assumptions, not new measurements. Use them to test a pipeline, as we used simulations throughout this course, not as evidence for a law. A generator can't measure. Only experiments can.

transcript.title: What comes next
transcript.text: Part five: what comes next. Discovery systems that plan experiments in real laboratories, with critics that know units, conservation and symmetry. Laws found across many systems at once, with parameters that change from case to case. Uncertainty reported as routinely as the formula. And benchmarks that test discovery, not memory. Some questions are still open: how to search when the right variables were never measured, and how to tell a law from a habit of one dataset. And when people and algorithms find a law together, who gets the credit? Each of those is a place where the habits of this course still apply: state the claim, test it where it could fail, and report what you find. And through all of it, the questions of this course: what do the data really say, what would refute this law, and how would anyone check it?

transcript.title: Recap
transcript.text: Let's recap. Distil a teacher inside the range where it learned, and report fidelity and accuracy separately. When you have the data, fit the data. A student explains its teacher, mistakes included. Symbolic features let simple models extrapolate. And generated data carry the generator's assumptions, not new evidence. In the lab, you'll distil a black box into a formula, and test it beyond the data. That's the end of the course. Thank you for discovering with us.

labs.title: Curve versus law
labs.text: Fit a polynomial and two drag laws to a falling ball's speed, stretch the window, and see which one survives. Then predict Uranus with Kepler's third law.
labs.intro: The data are simulated in your browser (quadratic drag, k₂ = 0.12 per metre, made up). Four challenges are checked as you go.
labs.card: A polynomial and two drag laws on falling-ball data; Kepler's law with Uranus held out.

labs.title: Expression workbench
labs.text: Type a formula and see its tree, prefix and postfix strings, size measures and sharing. Mutate branches, test two formulas for equivalence, check units, and count what survives the unit rules.
labs.intro: Everything is computed in your browser from your own formulas; the counts are exact. Four challenges are checked as you go.
labs.card: Trees, prefix and postfix, sharing, units and equivalence for formulas you type.

labs.title: Units guard
labs.text: Check drain-time formulas for a draining tank against their units, find dimensionless groups from a null space, slide a rule from soft to hard, and climb the knowledge ladder on your own simulated tanks.
labs.intro: The tank is simulated in your browser (Torricelli's law with a made-up discharge coefficient of 0.6). Four challenges are checked as you go.
labs.card: Units, dimensionless groups, soft and hard rules, and a ladder of knowledge for a draining tank.

labs.title: Search arena
labs.text: Race random search, size-ordered enumeration and a small genetic program on one budget to recover the range of a thrown ball. Change the budget, seeds, tournament size, crossover and noise, and watch the best error, the recovery rate and the Pareto front.
labs.intro: The throws are simulated in your browser (R = v²·sin 2θ / g with small noise), and each searcher runs here too. Four challenges are checked against the runs you make.
labs.card: Random search, enumeration and genetic programming race for the range law on one budget.

labs.title: Noisy derivatives
labs.text: Film a weight on a spring with a simulated phone: change the tracking noise, frame rate and windows, and watch finite differences, smoothing and a weak form recover (or lose) the law. Then choose the amplitude of the next swing to pin down a stiffening term.
labs.intro: The spring and the camera are simulated in your browser (a = −16·x − 0.4·v, made up). Four challenges are checked as you go.
labs.card: Finite differences, smoothing and weak forms on noisy video of a spring, and the next swing to record.

labs.title: Collapse and envelope
labs.text: Time nine pendulums on Earth, Mars and the Moon, and choose the axes until they fall on one curve; hang a heavy string and watch the collapse break. Then measure where a formula for the period holds, at the tolerance you choose, and refit it on wider swings.
labs.intro: The pendulums are simulated in your browser (exact periods from the elliptic integral, 0.5% timing noise; the heavy string makes the 1.2 m pendulums physical pendulums). Four challenges are checked as you go.
labs.card: Collapse nine pendulums onto one curve, break it with a missing variable, and measure a formula's validity envelope.

labs.title: Sparse dynamics
labs.text: Record a chemical clock from one or several starting mixtures, choose the noise, the pipeline and the threshold, and run sparse regression. Then put the feed into the library and test the law where the fit never looked: its steady state, the feed where it starts to tick, and its period at a feed nobody ran.
labs.intro: The clock is the Brusselator, a textbook model of oscillating reactions, simulated in your browser (readings every 3 s for 15 min, Gaussian noise). Four challenges are checked as you go.
labs.card: Find a chemical clock's law with sparse regression, and test it on steady states, the onset of ticking and a feed nobody ran.

labs.title: Field discovery
labs.text: Choose an experiment on the coast, the noise, the pipeline and the threshold, and run sparse regression on seven candidate field terms. See a window that watches one front invent a drift, find where the weak form stops working, and test the law you find on two releases that merge, an experiment the fit never saw.
labs.intro: The plant is simulated in your browser with the Fisher–KPP equation (sensors every 1 km, four readings a week for 24 weeks, Gaussian noise, closed ends). Four challenges are checked as you go.
labs.card: Find a spreading plant's field law from noisy sensors, and test it on two releases that merge.

labs.title: Stress-test bench
labs.text: Fit a draining tank's law with different pipelines and data, check whether the error bars are calibrated on 100 simulated experiments, run a negative control with shuffled readings and a positive control with a syrup, and choose the next experiment where three rival laws disagree most.
labs.intro: The tank drains through a small hole (Torricelli's law), simulated in your browser: a level sensor reads every 2 s with the noise you choose. Four challenges are checked as you go.
labs.card: Stress-test a tank law: calibration, controls, and the experiment that falsifies its rivals.

labs.title: Distil a black box
labs.text: Train a black box on a projectile's range, ask it questions inside or beyond its data, and fit a symbolic student to its answers. Compare fidelity with accuracy, see a student copy its teacher's mistakes, and use the formula you found as a feature for a straight line.
labs.intro: The shots are simulated in your browser (flat ground, no drag, the noise you choose), and both black boxes are trained there: a nearest-neighbour average and a degree-4 polynomial. Four challenges are checked as you go.
labs.card: Distil a black box into a formula, and test it beyond the data.
